div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.
MY DEAREST NELLIE,

Just at present, when most people are thinking 4f going int 6 the country to pay visits, or possibly planing out travels abroad, on either of which occasions it is not always convenient to take a maid, therefore the new invention which bas just been brought out will meet a long felt want. This invention is known as the "Pneumatic Handle," and consists of a roll of naturally curly hair, which can be easily pinned on to the head, forming the centre part of the fashionable coiled head-dress, and leaving the remainder of the hAir to be wound round it. This pneumatic handle is entirely made of hair extremely light and uncrushable, and, when it becomes rough, the re-dressing process- is most simple. A little wooden stick is slipped through the roil, which is hollow, and then the hair is brushed much in the same Nvay ;us a man's silk hat is brushed, or, if the wearer's hair is naturally curly hair, can be just rallied a little to look natural without, in the least spoil ing • it. Given a very small quantity of hair, and J. still smaller amount of skill in hairdressin,,, with the help of a pneumatic handle a smart e,4idnue can be achieved in a very few roinutes, and a well-dressed head is .of the utmost importane.e.

lvery pretty, yet nimple coiffure, suitable •cither for day or evening toilette, can have the front and side hair dote up at night on large wavers, and when released, drawn back over a small low Pompadour frizette, and fastened not too tightly. Unless the hair is very abundant, some .addition will be required to make the three puffs, but if there is a fair quantity, the two lower pus could be arranged from the natural hair, and one short fall tress would form the top, which is pinned much .loser to the head than the lower ones, which are caught more to the tisd part, and stand away „from . the head.

A very pretty-coat for small wearers iEvin rese,da or dull periwinkle-blue, and stole fronts and epau- lettes of ecru lace, forms a charming wra p for sum- mer wear. Roman satin is a smart, ri- eh-looking material for small people's wraps, and t also for babies' pelisses, but this same model c omes out -well in pique or cambric, trimmed with Swiss embroidery, or in white washing silk and soft lace. A most original little tea-jacket is made .of black striped chine silk, in shades of ;n 'Awe, g( raniurn, purple, is pretty, but the battleintinted re vers and cuffs of white silk, edged with ivory la( ied kit- tings, give quite .a novel effect. The v est and cravat are of ivory lace and the waist is el icircled by a belt of gold and turquoise, aratchi vg the little turquoise buttons which 114.11. hue& the revers.

I have lately seen Some very stylish pink cam. brie skirts, called "Cartha,," v•ery prettily trimmed with embroidered insertions • The smart, little model can be made in sky-blue. sau-desnil, and maize colour, and also in plain white. The smartest shoes for seaside and yachting this summer are of white canvas, with moderately high heels. They look very smart and pretty, and are delightfully comfortabie for proinenadingor boating, but unsuitable for walking far. In fact, well-fitting tan shoes are still the best for holiday wear. A cloth cape is as indispensable as a Cravenette waterproof cloak on a holiday tour in Great Britain, where one has hot sun one day and cold rain the next. A very useful cape of Cravenette cloth, which. as I daresay you know, is imvirvious to rain, and yet hasielothing mt.h e. in aneearance or ()leer to distinguish it free ordinary cloth. This design is easiest made in reeersible cloth, the plaid inner side in iking smart revers, whieh might be secured with large wrought buttons, and finished with shawl fringe, as shown. A smart tailor gown specially suitable for sea- side wear, is of blue serge, the coat made as a bodice, and the facings either white, ivory, or biscuit coloured cloth, with narrow blue or black braid. The collar lies flat over the shoulder, in- stead of standing up, as shown, imud at the back is wide and square. The vest is of soft white or creamy silk, and there are fancy filigree buttons in blue and gold. The skirt can, of course, be quite plain, but for a tall figere the broad border of light cloth, covered with lines if braid, is exceed- ingly effective. An entirelv new gpiel is of chen6 silk, or alpaca, the coat b Alice inaL with a prettily tubbed basque, finished with a lacc trill. and open- ing over a full vest of soft ivory silk or silk alpaca, held in with shoulder-straps of jewelled em- broidery. THE FORTUNATE BATH, "Heaven has to all allotted, soon or late, Some lucky revolution of their fate; Whose motions if we watch and guide with sial.l (For human good depends on human will) Our fortune rolls as from a smooth descent, And front the first impression takes its bent. Now, now she meets you with a glorious prize, And spreads her locks before her as she flies." —DRYDEN. Meanwhile, what had our young aelveuturer been doing in all these months between September and Traverse with his two hundred dollars had set out for New Orleans about the first of October.

By the time he had paid his travelling expenses and fitted himself out with a respectable suit of professional black, and a few necessary books, his little capital had diminished three quarters, So that when he found himself settled in his new office, in a highly respectable quarter of the city, be had but filly dollars and a few dimes left. ,A portion of this sum was expended in a cheap , sofs-bedstead, a closed washstand and a spirit-lamp • coffe-boiler, for Traverse determined to lodge in his • office and board himself—" which will have this • additional advantage," said the cheerful fellow to himself-4" for besides saving me from debt, it, will keepmealways on hand for calla." lAA.; wcugh it was October, had scarcely abated; indeed, on the contrary, it seemed to have revived and increased in virulency in consequence of the premature return of mlny people who had fled on its firte, appearance, and who in coming back too soon to the infected atmosphere, were less able to withstand contagion than those who re- mained. That Traverse escaped the plague was owing not so much to his favourite " theory " as to his vigor- ous constitution, pure blood, and regular habits of temperance, cieanliness, and cheerful activity of ; mind and Lociy. Just then the di msnd was greater than the supply , of medical service. Traverse fou-si plenty to do. And his pleasant young face and hop& u• and confident ; manners won him great favour in sick rooms, where, whether it were to be ascribed to his "theory'," his ; "practice," or to the happy influence of his personal preserc•-, or to all these together, with the blessing of the Lord upon them—it is certain that he was very successful in raising the sick. It is true that he did not earn five dollars in as many days; for his practice, like that of almost every young pro- fessional man, was among the indigent. But what of that 7—what if he were not running up heavy accounts against wealthy patrons 7—he was "giving to the poor "—not money, for himself Was as poor as any of them—but his time, labour, • and prctessional skill; he "was giving to the poor." he was "lending to the Lord," and he "liked the security." And the most successful speculator that ever made a fortune on 'Change, never, never : Invested time, labour, or money to a surer advan- tage. And this I would say for the encouragement of all young perscra in situilar circumstances—do not • be impatient if the " returns " are a little while delayed, for they are so sure and so rich that they are quite worth waiting for, nor will the waiting be long. Give your services cheerfully, also, for "the , Lord loveth a cheerful giver." Traverse managed to keep out of debt; he regu- larly paid his office rent and his laundress' bill; he daily purchased his mutton chop or pound of beef- steak, and broiled it himself; he made his coffee; swept and dusted his office; put up his sofa-bed; blacked his boots; and oh! miracle of indepen- dence, he mended his own gloves and sewed on his own shirt-buttons—for you may depend that the widow's son knew how to do all these things; nor was there a bit of hardship in his having so to wait upon himself, though if his mother and Clara, in their well-provided and comfortable home at Willow Heights, had only known how destitute the young man was of female aid and comfort how they would have cried! "No one but himself to mend his poor dear gloves! h—ob, boo-boo-oo I" Traverse never alluded to his straitened circum- stances; but boasted of the comfort of his quarters and the extent of his practice, and declared that his income already exceeded his outlay; which was perfectly true, since he was resolved to live within it, whatever it might be. As the fever began to subside, Traverse's practice declined, and about the middle of November his "occupation was gone." We said: that his office was in the most respec- table locality in the city; it was, in fact, on the ground floor of a first-class hotel. It happened that one night, near the close of winter, Traverse lay awake on his sofa-bedetead, turning over in his mind how he should contrive to make both ends meet, at the conclusion of the present term, and feeling as near despondency as it was possible tor his buoyant and God-trusting soul to be, when there came a loud ringing at his office- bell. This reminded him of the stirring days and nights of the, preceding autumn. He started up at once to answer the summons. "Who's there 7" "Is Doctor Rocke in 7" • "Yes, what's wantstd `V' •"A gentleman, sir, in tbe house here, sir, taken very bad, • wants • the doctor directly, room number 655."

"Very well, tI-will be with the gentleman imme- diately," answered Traverse, plunging his head into basin of cold water and drying it hastily. In five minutes Traverse was in the office of the •hotel, inquiring for a waiter to show him up to 555. One was or tered.tb attend him, who led the way 'up several flights of stairs, and around divers galleries, until he opened a door and ushered the .doctor immediately into the sick room. There was.a little, old, dried-up Frenchman in a blue night-cap, extended on a bed in the middle of the .room, and .covered with a white counterpane that hung close-to:his rigid form as to a- corpse. And there was a little, old, dried-up French. woman in &brown merino gown and a higin-crowned muslin epp, who hopped and chattered about the bed like a frightened magpie. "Owl Monsieur le Docteur !" she screamed, jumping at Traverse in a way to make him start back.; -4,0 a, Monsieur le Docteur 1 I am .vera happy you to see! Voila mon fiere! Behold my brother,! He is ail hais vera ill! he is deadile is Vera devil" " I hope not," said Traverse, approaching the bed.

" Behold! Mon Dieu, he is veratstill Ihe Is vcra cold! he is vera dead! what can you, ,mon frere. my brother to save 7" "Be composed, Madam, if you please, and allow me to examine my patient," said Traverse, taking the wrist of the sick man. "Ma foil I kuow not what you speak compose.' What can you my brother to save 7 "Mach, I hope, Madam, but you must leave me to examine my patient and not interrupt me," said Traverse, parish* his hand over the naked chest of the sick man. "Mon Dieu I I know not 'exam' and 'interrupt' and 1 know not what can you won here to saver "If you don't hash parley-vooing, the doctor can't nothink, main," said the waiter, in a respect- lal tone. Traverse found his patient in a bad condition..... In a stupor, if not in a state of positive insensi- bility. The surface of his body was cold as ice, and apparently without the least vitality. If he was net, as his sister had upraised it, "very dead," he was certainly "next to it." By close cinestioning, and by patting tie questions In various forms, the doctor learned from the chatter- ing little magpie of a Frenchwoman that the patient had been ill tor nine days; that he had been under the care of Monsieur le Ducteur Cartiere; that there had been a consultation of physicians; that they had prescribed for him and given him over; that to Dooteur Cartiere still attended him, but was at this instant in attendance as accoucbear to a lady in ex- treme danger, whom he could not leave; but Doc- tear Cartiere had directed then), in his unavoidable absence, to call in the skilful, the talented, the soon to be illustrious young Docteur Rocke, who was also near at hand. The heart of Traverse thrilled with joy. The Lord had remembered him. His hest skill spent upon the poor and needy who cculd make him no return, but whose lives he bad succeeded in saving, had reached the ears of the celebrated Dr. C., who had with the unobtrusive magnanimity of real genius, kindly recommended him to his own patrons. Ob, well, be would do his very best, not- only to advance his own professconal interests, and to pleased his mother and Clara, hut also to do honour to the magnanimous Dr. C.'s recommenda- tion.
Here, too, was an opportunity of putting ih practice hi 4 favourite theory ; but first of all it was necessary to be informed of the preceding mode of treatmgat and its results.

' So he farther questioned the little, restless mag- pie, and by ingeniously framed inquiries, succeeded in gaining from her the necessary knowledge of his patient's antecedents. He examined all the Inedi ines that had been used, and informed himself of their effects upon the disease. But the most serious difficulty of all, seemed to be, the Impossibility of raising vital action upon the cold, dead skin.

The chattering little woman informed him that the patient had been covered with blisters that would not "pull," that would not a decliniate," that would not, what you call it—" drawl" Traverse could easily believe this, for not only the skin, but the very flsh of the old Frenchman seemed bloodless and lifeless. Now for his theory! what would kill a healthy man with a perfect circulation, might save the life of this dying one, whoso stole surface, inch deep, seemed already dead. "Put him in a bath of mustard water, as hot as you can bear your own hand in, and continue to 'raise the temperature slowiy, watching tne effect for about five minutes. I will go down and prerare a cordial draught to be taken the moment he get:: back to bed," said Doctor Backe, who immediately left the room.

His directions were all but too well obeyed. The bathing tub was quickly brought into the chamber and filled with water, as hot as the nurse could bear her hand in. Then the invalid was hastily invested in a sli4ht bathing gown and lifted by two servants and laid in the hot bath. "Now, bring quickly, water boiling," said the little, old woman, imperatively. Aud when a large copper kettle full was forthcoming, she tbok it and began to pour a stream of hissing, bubbling water In at the foot of the bath.

The skin of the torpid patient had been reddening for a few seconds, SO as to prove teat its sensibility was returning, and now when the stream from the kettle began to mix with the already very hot bath, and the patient, with the agility of ycnth and health, skipped out of the tub and into his bed, kicking vigorously, and exclaiming: "Brigands I assassins I you have scalded my legs to deatn I"
"Glory be to the Lord! he's saved I" cried one of the waiters, a devout Irishman. " Ciel 1 he speaks I be moves! ho lives! MO7l Mrs 1" cried the little Freuchwomiin, going to him.

" Ah, murderers! bandits! you've scalded me to deilth I I'll have you all before the commiasairel" "lie scolds! he threatens 1 he swears he gets well awn Irere 1" cried the old woman, busying kerself to change his clothes and put on his flinnel night-gown. They then tucked him up warmly in bed, and put bottles of hot water all around, to keep up this newly stimulated circula- tion. _ _ _

At that moment Dr. Rocks came in, put bis hand Into the bath-tab, and could scarcely repress a cry of pain and of horror—the water scalded his fingers! what must it have done to the sick man! "Good heaven, Madam? I did not tell you to parboil your patient 1" exclaimed Traverse, speaking to the old woman. Traverse was shocked to find bow perilously his orders had been executed. "Eh hien, Monsieur! he lives! he does well! . ..

Voila mon tr erel" exclaimed the little old woman. It was true! the accidental "boiling bath," as it might almost be called, had effected what perhaps no other means in the world could—a restored circulation. _ _

The disease was broken up and the convalescence of the patient was rapid. And as Traverse kept his own secret concerning the accidental high tempera- ture of that bath, which every one considered a fearful and a successful experiment, the fame of Dr. Rocke spread over the whole city and country. He would soon have made a fortune in New Orleans, had not the hand of destiny beckoned him elsewhere. It happened thus: The old Frenchman whose life Traverse had partly by accident and partly by design succeeded in saving, comprehended perfectly well bow narrow his escape from death had been, and attributed his restoration solely to the genius, skill and boldness of his young physician, and was grateful accordingly with all a Frenchulan't noisy demonstration. He called Traverse his friend, his deliverer, his lOU One day, as soon as he found himself strong enough to think of pursuing his journey, he called his "son" into the room and explained to him that he, D3ctor Pierre St. Jean, was the proprietor of a private Insane Asylum, very exclusive, very quiet, very aristocratic, indeed, receiving none but patients of the highest rank; that this retreat was situated on the wooded banks of a charming lake In one of the most healthy and beautiful neigh- bourhoods of East Feliciana ; that he had originally come down to the city to engage the services of some young physician of talent as his assistant, and finally, that he would be delighed I enraptured! if "his deliverer I his friend I his son!" would accept the post. Now Traverse particularly wished to study the various phases of mental derangement, a depart- ment of his professional education that had hither- to been opened to him only through books. He explained this to his old friensi, the French physician, who immediately wet off into ecstatic exclamations of joy as, "Good 1 Great 1 I Grand f' and "I shall now repay my good child! .my dear son I for his so excellent skill I" The terms of the engagement were soon arranged, and Traverse prepared to accompaty his new friend to his "beautiful retreat," the private mad-house. But first .Traverse wrote to his mother and to Clara in Virginia, and alsf, to Herbert.Grepon In hiexic% .40 apprise them of his good fortune.

—M. G. LEWIfb.

It was at the close of a beautiful day in early spring that Traverse Rocke, accompanying the old doctor and the old sister, reached the grove on the :borders of the beautiful lake upon the banks of which was situated the "Calm Retreat."

A large, low, white building, surrounded with piazzls and shaded by fragrant and fliwering eouthern trees, it looked like the luxurious country ,reat of some wealthy merchant or planter, rather than a prison for the insane. Doctor St. Jean conducted his young assistant Into a broad and cool hall, on each side of which •doots opened into spacious rooms, occupied by the proprietor and his household. The cells of the patients, as it rzppeared, were upstairs. The country doctor and the matron who had been in charge during the absence of the proprietor and his sister, now came forward to welcome the party, and report the state of the institution and its in- Mates. All were as usual, the ,Country doctor said, except 44 Id Ale moiselle." 6• And what of her, how is Mademoiselle I—A patient most interesting, Doctor R )cke ?" said the old Fcenchtnan, ail ernatek, questiuLaug his substi- tute and atidrcssing Traverse. "She has stopped her violent ravings, and seems to me to be ed,king izto a stupid despair," replied the substitute. - - - -

"A pattent most interesting, n y young friend! a history most pathetic; you sball bear of it some time. But come into the parlour. And you, Angels, my sister, ring, and order ccffee," said the old Frenchman, lemling the way into a pleasant apartment on the right of the ball, furnished with straw matting upon the floor, and bamboo settees and chairs around the walls.

Here coffee was presently served to the travellers, who soon after retired for the Dig!it. Traverse's room was a large, pleasant apartment at the end of a wide, long hall, on each side of whieh were the tloo:s opening into the cells of the patients. Fatigued by his journey, Traverse slept soundly through tbe night; but early in the morning he was rudely awakened by the sounds of maniac voices from the cells. Some were crying, some laughing aletd, some groaning and howling, and some holding forth in fancied exlv_mations. He dressed himself quickly and lett the room, to walk down the length or the long hall and observe the cells on each aide. The doers were at regular intervals, and each door had in its centre a small opening to ehaOle the prop; ieLur to look in upon the patients. _ _

, As these were all women, and some of them delicate and refined even in their insanity, Traverse felt shock:A at this necessary, if it were necessary, exsure of their anetuary. The cells were in fact small bed rooms, that with th,ir white- wcislied ivalls, and white curtained beds and windows, looked excessiv<-1? neat, clean and cool, but also, it mast be contessed, very bioa, dreary and cheerless. Even,a looking.glass would be a great benefit to those poor girls, for I remember that even Clara, in I bee violent grief, and mother in her life-long sorrow never neglected their looking-glass, and personal gopearancet'Lsaiti Traverse to himself. as he passed

down the hall, and received that this • gence should be afforded the patients. THE MAN WHO KNO .vS [-- dog tile And except those first involuntary glances, he He drive:, directly home, even in dark nishta Bcrupulously avoided looking in through the n k 1T ver-lieneing 1 Ina w news t road. he eds. do gratings upon those helpless women who had no meacs of secluding themselves. I the deceptive shadows, the uncertain sou" ' Oer his le 17" But as he turned to go down the stairs, his eyes bother him. He can feel the ground ue • e ;4 went lull into an opposite cell, and reit upon a wheels, and the" lay of the land "is (Wn teee e vitio vision of I beauty and sorrow that immediately a. Parts dt clear noontide. It is the stranger in tho_ , up toe- rivetted his gaze. and befuddledie It was a small and graceful female figure, clothed I confused ' who knocks eteeP In deep black, seated by the window, with her I questions, who finally lodges in the ditch. elbow resting upon the sill and her chin supported on her hand. Her eyes were cast down until her eye-lashes lay like inky lines upon her snow-white cheek e Her face, of classic regularity and marble whiteness, bore a ghastly contrast to the long eye- lashes, arched eye-brow and silken ringlets, black as midnight. She might have been a statue or a picture, so motionless she sat. 008SCiOUS of the wrorg of gazing upon this solitary woman, Traverse forced his looks away and passed on down stairs, where he again met the old dector and Mademoiselle Angele at breakfast. After breakfast, Doctor St. Jean invited his young assistant to accompany him on a round of visits to the patients, and they went immediately up to the hall, at the end of which Traverse had slept. "These are our incurables, but they are not vio- lent; incurables never are. Poor Mademoiselle! si.e has just been conveyed to this ward," said the doctor, opereng the door of the first cell on the right at the head of the stairs, and admitting Tra- verse at once into the presence of the beaune al, black-haired, snow-faced woman, who had so much Interested him. `•Th:s is my friend, Doctor Rocke, Mademoiselle ; Doctor, this is my friend, Mademoiselle Mont De St. P:erre." Traverse bowed profoundly, and the lady arose, curtsied and resumed her seat, saying coldly: "I have told you, Mousier, never to address me as Mademoiselle; you persist in doing so; and I shall never notice the insult again." "Ten thousand pardons, Madame! but if Madame will always look so young so beautiful ! 0411 I ever remember that she is a widow ? " The classic lip of the woman curled in scorn, and she disdained a reply. "I take an appeal to Monsier Le Doctenr—ls not Madame young and beautiful " asked the Frenchman, turning to Traverse, while the splendid black eyes of the stranger passed from one to the other. Traverse caught the glance of the lady and bowed gravely. It was the most delicate, and proper reply. She smiled almost as gravely, and with a much kinder expression than any she had bestowed upon the Frenchman. "And how has Madame fared during my absence so long? The servants—have they been respectful 7 have they been observant have they been obedit,nt to the will of Madame? Madame has but to speak!" said the doctor, bowing politely. "Why should I speak when every word I utter you believe, or affect to believe, to be the ravings of a maniac? / will speak no more," said the lady, turning away her superb dalk eyes and looking oat of the window. "Ah, Madame will not so punish her friend, her servant 1 her slave 1" A gesture of fierce impatience and disgust was the only reply deigned by the lady. "Come away; she is angry and may become dan- gerously excited," said the old doctor, leading the way from the cell. Did you tell me this lady is one of the Inca- ables 7" inquired Traverse, when they left her apartment. "Bah I yes, poor, vera incurable, as my sister would say." "Yet, she appears to me to be perfectly sane, as well as exceedingly hemp :fat and interesting," "Ah, bah 1 my excellent; my admirable; my inexperienced young friend, tnat is all you know of lunatics. With more or less violence of assertion, they every one insist upon their sanity; just as criminals protest their innocence 1 Ah, bait! you shall go into every cell in this ward, and not find one lunatic among them," sneered the old doctor, as he led the way into the next little room. It was indeed as he had foretold, and Traverse Rocke found himself deeply affected by the melancholy, the earnest, and sometimes the violent manner in which the poor unfortunates protested their sanity, and implored or demanded to be restored to home and triends. "You perceive," said the doctor, with a dry laugh, "that they are none of them crazy I" "I see," said Traverse, "but I also detect a very great difference between that lovely woman in the south cell and these other inmates. "Bah! bah! bah! she is more beautiful! more accomplished! more refined than the others, and she is in one of her luoid intervals 1 that is all! but as to a difference between her insanity and that of other patieets, it lies in this, that she is the most hopelessly mad of the whole lot. Sue has been mad eighteen years! "Is it possible I" exclaimed Traverse. incredu- lously. "She lost her reasoe at the age of sixteen, and she is thirty-tens—you can calculate I" "It Is ausszing and very soreowful 1 how beauti- ful she is!" " Yes ; her beauty was a fatal gift It is a sad story! Ah, it is a sad story! You shall hear of it when we get through." "I can connect no idea of woman's frailty with that refined and intellectual face," said Traverse, coldly. "Ah, bah! you are young you know not the world I you! my innocent, my excellent, my pious young friend 1" said the old doctor, as they crossed the hall to eo into the next wing of the building, In which were situated the men's wards. Traverse hound nothing that particularly interested him in this department,, and when they had concluded their round of visits, and were seated toeether in the old doctor's study, Traverse asked him for the story of his beautiful patient. The doctor shrugged his shoulders. "It is a story miserable, as I told you before. A gentleman, illustrious, from Virginia, an officer high in the army, and distinguished in the war, he brought this woman to me nearly three years ago. He informed me that --eh hien 1 I had better tell you the story in my own manner. This young lady, Mademoiselle Mont de St. Pierre, is of a family uoble and distinguished—a relative of this officer, illustrious and brave. At fifteen, Mademoi- selle met a man, handsome and without honor. Ah, bah! you under. tend !at ter een the child became a fallen angel! See lost her reason through sorrow and shame! This relative—this gentleman, illustri- ous and noble, tender and compassionate—took her too the sconision of his country house, where she lived in elegance, luxury and honour. But as the years passed nor malady iocreas.eci ; her presence became dangerous ; in a word, the gentleman, dis- tinguished and noble, saw tee advertisement of my 'calm retreat,' my institution incomparable, and be wrote to me. In a word, he trawl ray terms, and brought to me his young relative, so lovely and 80 i;0 is a good m in, this officer so gallant, so chivalrous; bui she is ungrateful!" "Ungrateful 1" "Au, bah 1 'yes; it is the way with lnnatles 1 They eve 7 iru teine Oasis beat friemis to be their worst enennee I Tee poor, cr zsd creature fancies that she is the sister-in-law f this officer Llustrious she thiues that she is tee widow of his elder brother, whom she imagines he murdered, and that she is the mether of children whom she says he has abducted or destroyed, so . that he may enjoy the estate that is her widow's dower and their orphans' patrimo -y! That is the reason why she insists on being. celled Madame instead of Mademoi- selle, and we nuinlee her when we think of it." "But all this is very singular "Ah, bali 1 who can account for a lunatic's fan- cies? She is the maddest of the whole lot I Some- times she need to become so violent that we would have to restrain het 1 B letely, Doctor Wood tells me, she is qtat,t ; that we cot seder a had sign; there is alwab hope io,' mtnatica lintel they begin to sit k into this state," eaid the doctor, with an air of cora:yeti:Ley. The exodus of the great schools from the metro- polis to the cinintry is still in progress, and the military authorities have under consideration a scheme for transferring the Duke of York's school for the sons of soldiers from Chelsea, where it now stands, to some rural spot where the children would be brought up under healthier conditions. The transference will give the military authorities a noble site for barracks, and it would be wort", knowing whether it is the health of the children or the possession of the site which makes the War Office so keen an advocate of the change.

Mr. William Black is the subject of a long study in the August " Young \tan." Besides his club, the novelist now has a oied a terre in London in the shape of some cl ;-facllioned chambers at the Embankment end of BucLingham-street. Peer the Great once lived in these rooms, and they are sup- posed to have been the dwelling-place for a time of David Copperfield. in them, moreover, Mr. Black himself has laid some of the scenes of" Sunrise." Mr. Black tells us that not a few of his readers have remonstrated with him upon the " sad endings" which he has given to several of his novels. Even the late President Garfi-dd, it seems, was not super- ior to ttrk amiable weakness for" poetical justice" in our fiction. One summer, hearing from Mr. Carnegie that he was going to Scotland and would !I call Upon William Black. the President asked him. to take a message to the novelist. Garfield reproached him for the conclusion of " Macleod of , Dare," pathetically adding, " Was there not enough I sorrow in the world ?"

A very small model of the lightning expresa rail- way invented by Mr F. B. Beyer was shown in working order on Monday. The permanent way may be briefly described as a development of the Lartigue single-rail system used in building the line from Listowel to Ballybunion. The line de- signed by Mr. Beyer is constructed with much greater solidity,and is provided with double guide- rails in order to meet the enormous pressure under wtich his proposed trains would be worked in their progress at 120 to 150 miles an hour. To enable them to pass round sharp curves speedily and safely Mr. Beyer designs his carriage in two or more se- parate parts, identical in build, and joined together by a pivot or " universal joint. Mr. Beyer ex- plained that the trains would of necessity be short, but practically unlimited in frequency. Stoppages would have to be minimised in order to avoid the delay involved in frequent starts and slowings. Be hcped his invention would be utilised by existing railways for their express traffic, and showed that his line could be built alongside or, if necessary. above the present iron roads.

Two important Nonconformist pastorates have now to be filled up. One is that of Bloomsbury Chapel. Mr. Baillie, has preached his farewell tder- mons, and the deacons are anxiously looking out for a suitable successor to a rather difficult, though by no means discouraeing post. The Presbyterians are still without a minister at the handsome church in Westbourne-grove. Dr. Walter Morison, the late minister, has settled in S,otland, and though many "supplies " have occupied the pulpit, no one has been called. I hear, however, that the Rev. J. Smyth Wood, of Sunderland, has created a very favourable impression, and may possibly be invited to come to London.

It is stated that one at least of the Irish landlords in the House of Commons has received very strong protests from his constituents against his action in opposing the passage of the Irish Land Bill, and that he is more than half doubtful as to the recep- tion which he will get when he visits his constitu- ency in the autumn. This is, no doubt, one of the considerations which have operated to make the Irish Unionists cautious about taking any open steps to kill the bill. Many of them, indeed, have preferred to keep their own speeches within bounds, leaving the most hostile speeches against the bill to be made by Mr. Carson, who represents a University constituency, and has therefore nothing to fear from popular opinion. However, as Mr. Carson is the representative of the Landlords' Com- mittee, and has only moved such amendments as the Committee agreed to, it would be a mistake to consider him as acting merely in his peroonal capacity. This is a fact which the Ulster farmers are probably luite shrewd enough to appreciate.

Mr. William Johnston has given notice o ask the First Lord of the Treasury "whether, con- sidering that by the 23rd of September the Qtie.n will have reigned for a longer perio 1 than any of her predecessors on the throne, the Government will consider the propriety of having a special form of thanksgiving prepared, to be used on that day and on the following Sunday,in devout recognition. of the favour of Almighty God shown to the Em- pire during the continuance of Her Majesty's long and happy reign" The question stands on the paper tor Thursday, but Mr. Johnston has,at, Mr:Balfour's request, agreed to postpone it till Monday. This rather looks as though the First Lord of the Trea- sury may have some statement to make on the sub- ject., although he may not be prepared to accept _Mr. Johnston's suggestion. The proposal that the event referred to in the question should he marked in some special and official form is known to be favoured in very influential quarters.

"Colonel Saunderson is so widely recognised as a Parliamentary force, a statesman of singularly judicious mind, as to obscure, the bent of his natural genius," says Mr. H. W. Lucy, 'facetiously, in the "Strand Magazine." He goes on to say that if the Colonel were not a statesman he would be a boat- builder. "As it is, he manages to steal some hours, even days, from political duties to planning and building ships. From the inception to the launch- ing, he does it all himself; or, where he takes on assistance. he personally supervises the labour. He has trained a local carpenter with such success that between them they can turn out a yacht seaworthy from keel to mast-head. The Colonel also plans the engines, though that is necessarily work the carry- ing out of which must be committed to other hands. As he never sells a boat, and is always building, he has quite a fleet under his flag."

An American magazine supplies the latest item in the progress of " Emancipation" :—Mrs. Mary L. Foote,recently elected the police justice of Gaylord, Kan., ran against her husband and defeated him by a large majority. Comment is absolutely needless. But it may be remarked that the name " Gaylord " under the circumstances seems a sorry irony.

Princess Li, the wife of Li Hung Chang, is fifty years old,but is said to look twenty years younger. Her feet have ly.en fashioned to such smallness that she cannot walk, and has to 1)e carried about in a chair,a magnificent one, of caurse—yet she owns a thouQand pairs of shoes. Th-kr husband's wealth enables her to have nearly one thousand silk dresses, and she can select from five hundred fur garments in winter.

With reference to the Royal marriage this !reek the English home of the newly wedded pair will be kvpleten Hall, about a mile from Sandringham, whilst their Danish home near Copenhagen is calkd " Sorgen-fri." At Appleton the honeymoon will he spent. The Crown Prince of Denmark. is very wealthy, and is allowing his son £12,000 a year, whilst Princess Maud is to hare an income of .£4,000 a year out of tl'e allowance granted by Par- liament in 1889 for the family of the Prince of Presents,of course, have been pouring in, till they numbered about 500. The Queen's wed- ding gift consists of nearly a hundred rubies and diamonds set as an ornament. The Prince and Princess of Wales have given her a magnificent tiara of diamonds and pear-shaped pearls.
The calendar of the Liverpool Assizes, which com- mence on Monday next contains the names of forty-four p!isoners, of whom five are charged with murder and SIX with manslaughter.

div.head: TUE EX M rIV ER, SATUR DAY JULY 25, 1896.
div.p: TUE EX M rIV ER, SATUR DAY JULY 25, 1896.

rnary at a quarter to ten in the evening. Prisoner stepped int-i the lobby, but remained in the shadow. He said he had been sent up by M. po.ky to tell the family abaut the bicycle accid,nt, and th it Mr. Powley, who was near the Rain lan, nted to see them. Ask,--d by witness if 1-v‘ knew or had seen Mr. P.w:ey, he said, " N '" but that he had been sent in by the landiord of tit, inn. Mrs. Kace asked prisoner to sit down whilst witness went upstairs to put on a bonnet. Mrs. Kaye urged her to go at once. Witness left the hous- with her son,a daughter, and the accuseil,leaving Mrs. Kaye alone with another daughter aged eight,who was upstairs asleep. Before leaving she asked Mrs. KLye if she (deceased) was wit afraid to be left by herself. Mrs. K Lye replied that her fear was for Mr. Po wley. At the end of the footpath leading to the village prisoner left them,sayinc, he was going to Not- tingham. Finding that her husband was not at the inn witre,ss sent her son to find a policeman, and then go home. She did this suspecting that something was wron::. Having bind her husband in the committee. room in the village she returned with him. She found Mrs. Kaye injured and the house pillaged. This witness also identifio the watch and chain and other stolen valuables produced by the prosecution, and stated that the kitchen poker,which she had used about an hour be- fore the murder, was then straight. Afterwards it was bent and bloorls!-ained. In referring to this and other detail aof the affair already particularised by her bus- band,Mrs. Powley was with difficulty prevented from .fainting, and there was a painful pause in consequence. The cross examination was designed to thr•iw doubt on the exact ideiitity of the watch and other articles. Witness was asked to pick out the accused from among other men, but was ill and did not very well remember the occasion. Mr. Cracroft : Did not you point to a man who was not the prisoner and say to him, "Oh, the villain?" Witness: I don't remember. _ _ . .

- _ Police-constable T.irton, who was the first to enter the housio after the murder, described the state of the kitchen as he found it. Mrs. Kaye was lying on the door, her head close to the tender. Be lifted her on to the sofa, and sent for a doctor. She had blood on her hands, althoeigh they were not cut as far as he could see. Be discovered the bent poker on the floor of one of the front bedrooms. There were wet bloodstains upon it w en he pinked it up. The Judge: Did you show Mr. and Mrs. Powley the plker ? Witnecs : I did not.

The Judge: Why. Witness: they were excited about other things. Dr. William Lamb, practising at Arnold, detailed the results of the post-mortem. Mrs. Kaye had a fracture extending right across the skull, which was splintered. The brain substance had been badly bruised. On the left side of the head was a large abrased wound extend- ing from the front to the back of the skull, as well as four smaller contused wounds; two other wounds ap- peared on the right side of the head. The Judge: Each would be caused by a separate blow. Dr. Lamb: Certainly. All the wounds penetrated to the bone. The bones of the left hand were broken. Bruises also appeared on the arms and shoulders. Cross examined : There had evidently been a struggle between Mrs. li,ye and her assaila,nt,but the kitchen,as witness saw it when sent for by Turton, did not show that it had been violent. After corroborative medical evidence, an ostler at the Royal Oak Inn, was called to seeak of the accused changing his coat and vest at that inn on February 15'11, and leaving the old ones. This wit- ness was unable, however, to positively identify the prisoner. An assistant to a pawnbroker in Carrington-street, Nettingham, said prisoner on February 12 pledged there a tin box full of clothes,and redeemed them on the morn- ing of February 15. Witness stated in cross-examination that on an average 150 people came into the shop elaily. Prisoner was not a customer. A cloakroom assistant at the Central Station,Manches- ter, was next called, and spoke to prisoner leaving the box at the left luggage office. Alfred Turner, keeper of the Tank Inn, Longsight, Manchester, deposed that prisoner had drinks at that house from the 15th to the 23rd of Februaryeand on three occasions changed a soviireem. Samuel Ashton, formerly a fellow-employee of the prisoner on the railway at Manchester, said he met him at the Tank Inn, on the 20th February. Wilkinson offered to sell witness a silver watch and gold chain. Witness bought it from him for 7. 61, and sold it the same day for 10e. (Laughter.) Prisoner told him that since leaving Manchester he had lived at Sheffield. This:part of the case was strengthened by corrobora- tive evidence. James Thompson,licensee of the public-house in Stock- port-road. Manchester, said the prisoner, when in his hous, on the 22nd February, offered for sale a gold brooch set with blue stones (one of the stolen valuables) and a silver chain. The latter he sold for is. te a butler named Elwiss, who was now called. The prosecution concluded their case with police evi- dence bearing on the prisoner's arrest, the principal wit- ness being Superintendent Harrep, of the Nottingham police. Dr. Ranson, of Nottingham, waft also called as to the stains on the coat and vest left at the Royal Oak by the prisoner. These on analysis proved to be bloodstains. They were mixed with short dark grey hairs, which in his opinion were human. Cross-examined, witness said that human hair could only be distinguished from that of a horse or a dog by its smaller diameter, but he ad- mitted that the thickest human hair exceeded the thin- nest horse or dog hair. No witnesses were called for the defence, and Mr. Hetherington Smith proceeded to sum up for the Crown. He commented minutely and at length on the completeness of the chain of circum- stance which the prosecution had adduced. The only criestion that remained was that of identity, but he urged that where, as in the case of Mrs. Fawley, there appeared some hesitation on that point, the corroborative facts were too strong to be put aside. As half-past five Mr. Cracroft rose to deliver his speech for the defence, and the prisoner who,during the day had sat quietly in the dock, wearing a haggard and carewo n look, but giving no sign of movement beyond a nervous fidgetting of the hands, followed his counsel's observations witk the utmost attention. Mr. Cracroft commented, in the first place, on the difficulty of the defence. Be euegested next that Mrs. Kaye was killed not before,but after,the robbery, and during an attempt on her part to arrest the thief. With that view,he asked the jury not to rely upon the evidence of the police- man Turban that the p ler was found in the bedroom. There could, he admitted, be no doubt that accused on the 14th of February was in Arnold, and at the Ram Inn, but, knowing that Mr. Powley was a market gardener, and being himself a gardener, prisoner desired to go to Powley'e with the object of asking for employment. Coming next to the question of identity, he laid stress on the hesitation of several of the wit- nesses, and those among the most important, whilst on , the other hand the accused appeared to be mos: posi- tively identified by persons who had only seen him casu- I ally, and to whom he was a complete stranger. He urged, in conclusion, that the crime had not been broteeht home to the prisoner. The summing-up occupied about half-an-hour only. , Mr. Justice Grantham pointed out that the robbery at Pewley's house was e.vidently carefully planned by the thief, and would have succeeded but for Mrs. Kaye, whose visit was not known in the village, and whom the thief did not expect to encounter. Next day the same man was getting rid of a blood-stained coat and vest, and then there was the fact that the prisoner sold a watch ' and chain,whie.h there was really no doubt was part of the property stolen. In that particular instance, the prisoner's identity was beyond noubt, for he disposed of the watch and chain to an old fellow workman who knew him perfectly. Had the prisoner not stolen those article's evidence could have been called by him to show how he got them. If the prisoner was the man who com- mitted the robbery, he undoubtedly was also the man who committed the murder. ,The evidence was, there- fore, as clear and consecutive as it could well be. The jury retired, but a few minutes & liberation sufficed for them to make up their minds. They found the prisoner guilty, and the judge, assuming the black cap, sentenced him to death in the usual form, remark- ing that it was one of the most brutal murders it had ever been his lot to try, and hat the prisoner's fate ought to be a warning to all who were tempted to try a career of crime. Wilkinson was then assisted to the cells. Though his demeanour was impassive, it was evident that he suffered acutely.

div.head: TM- MURDER OF A WARRIN ,TON WOMAN.
div.p: TM- MURDER OF A WARRIN ,TON WOMAN.
ASSIZE-TRIAL AT NOTTINGRAM.
CONVIC LION AND DEATH SEN ChNCE.

On Monday. Samuel Wilkinson, aged f )rty-eight, gardener, was arraigned before Mr. Justice Grantham, at the Ns Assizes, for the murder ot Marc K AV?, at Arnold, a hamlet outside of Nottingham, on the 17th of February last. The victim belonged to Warrington,being only on a visit to Nottingham at the time of the murder. The court was crowded and a large number of persors assembled outside the courthouse. For !he Crown there appeared Mr. Hetherington Smith and Mr. Forkiham;-Mr. R. W.Craerset appeared fo! the prisoner. l'he prisoner, a man of slight build with hair turning grey, made the plea of not guilt y iii a scarcely a.unibls epise. Mr. fletherineton Smith opened the case for the Crown, and informed the jury that the evidence for the prosecution wa wholly circum;tantial he thousht it would leave no reasonatile doubt as to the guilt of the accused. He proceeded to explain that the deceased woman was discovered un- conscious from the serious injuries she had received in the kitchen of a lonely house known as King's Head Well, at Arnold. The house was 300 yards away from the nearest ,iwelling. and 500 cards from the main street through Arnold. The access to it from the main road was through a footpath running between high hedge- rows known as Moor End. Ihe house was occupied by Mr. Samuel Powley, market gardener, and his family. The old lady who was murdered was a visitor at the house. On the evening of the 14th February Mr. Pow- ley, who was a candidate for the Local Board, went in- to the village to prosecute his canvass. He went into the bar of the Ram's Inead.where he saw the prisoner. Tike latter had been seen in Ar,nold earlier in the day going along the road to Mansfield, and it would be proved that he asked for assistance at a house in the Man-field-read after that, so he must have returned to Arnold. for he was at the Rim's Head at nine o'clock. Prisoner asked some questions as to who 7dr. Powley was, and fiading out where Mr. P issley lived, the prosecution suggested that he went to King's Head Well for the purpose of rob- bery. Evidence would be adduced tracing the prisoner from the Rim's Head towards Powles's house. A witness would be called to prove that he directed prisoner to Powley's house. That was about a (pester to ten. It was about that time that a man came to the doer and inquired for Mrs. Powley, whom Mrs. Powley recognised as the prisoner. This man,whom the prosecution alleged was the accused, informed the people at the house that Mr. Powley had been knocked down in the village by a bicycle,and was badly ilijurecliand wanted all the family to go down to the Ram's Head. It was in this way that Mrs. Kaye came to be left in the house alone. Of course it was discovered when the family arrived at the Ram's Head that the story was a concoction. Suspecting then that something was wrong, the police were communicated with, and a constable went to the house immediately to find Mrs. Kaye unconscious on the floor of the kitchen, the house ransacked, and valuables in money and jewellery stolen. Some of thsse articles, counsel went on to say, would be traced to the prisoner's possession very shortly after. words. It would be remembered that on the 14th prisoner was begging on the high road. On the 15th he redeemed a box a clothins which he had previouely pledged in Nottingham, paying for it in gold coin. Shortly after that he entered the Royal Oak Inn, Broad- marsh, Nottingham, and changed his coat and vest, leaving his old vest and coat behind him. That dis- carded coat and vest were bloodstained. The next that was heard of him was that the sameevening,at Manches- ter.he left the b ,x of clothes at a railway station passel office. The next link in the chain was the fact that pri- soner, whilst in a public-house called the Tank Inn, at Manchester, sold a silver vat and gold chain, now ichentified as part ef the property stolen from Mrs. Powley,at Arnold. A second watch shain had also, in a similar manner,been traced to the accused. On the 23c 1 February prisoner was taken into custody at Manches- ter. He had then in his possession a railway parcel ticket relating to a box of clothing, and a key which opened the box The box contained a pair of trousers which the prosecution suggested were worn by the pri- soner when the murder took place at Arnold. The crime had evidently twee committed with a poker found at King's Head Well, arid bent owing to the violence with which it had been used. It happened that the fact of the prisoner having left his coat at the Royal Oak Inn was discovered by 'he prisoner himself asking, when charged with the crime, " Have you got my coat and vest from the" Royal Oak e Evidence for the Crown was then called, and plans were produced showing the situation of and access to Mr. Powley's house at Arnold, as well as the internal arrangements of the dwelling. After cross-examination on these planswith a view to show that it would be difficult to leave Powley's house altogether unobserved, the evidence was adduced of Annie Vernon, the woman from whom the prisoner asked assistance on the road towards Mansfield on the afternoon of February 14. The witness being unable personally to attend owing to illness, her depositions

were read. Harriet Perry, wife of a collier living at Arnold. also spoke to seeing the prisoner near the Ram Inn n the afternoon of Fe'xiiary 14, and she saw him again the same evening standing on the steps of the inn. It was about nine o'clock. and he was talking to Mr. Powley. She did not see him again until he seas brought before the magistrates. Samuel Powley, who was then put into the witness box, said that his house stood by itself, in a field, and was approached from Arnold by a footpath. He went into the village on February 14 at about half-past seven in the evening,leaving at home his wife, son.two daugh- ters, and Mrs, Kaye. On reaching the village he went into the RAM lan to canvass. While he was in the bar the prisoner entered. It was then about nine. The pri- soner asked for him (witness),and he was pointed out to him. When he went out the accused followed him. Wit- ness asked him for his support in the election. Be had a good view of 'he prisoner in the light of the lamp over the door. Wirness was in company with a Mr. Oliver, another candidate, and he was talking to that, gentleman as to where they would go next. The prisoner could have overheard the conversation. He remembered saying to Mr. Oliver that h. (wit- neas was going to the committee•room at Flufton and it was time that they were off. It was whilst walk- ing to Hutton that he was overtaken by his wife, who spoke about the supposed bicycle accident. He went straight home after that, and found the house in charge of a police-constable. Mrs. Kaye was lying in the kit- chen saturated with blood from a large wound in the forehead. A large pool of blood was on the flint near the hearthstone, which was extensively bloodstained. Blood to the extent of about a cupful, as witness had estimated, had lodged in a hole in the hearth. Mrs. Kaye was quite une.onecious. She died two days after- wards. Witness identified the silver watch and gold chain. These were stolen from a drawer in the bedroom. Money was also taken to the amo ,nt of £7. Cross-examiited.—There was not only blood on the hearth and firor of the kitchen, but blood- stains on all the walls, especially on the wall over the sofa. Until he saw prisoner at the Ram Inn he had not seen him previously. He did not suggest that prisoner knew where Hnfton was Prisoner did not tell him that he (accused) was a gardener. Mrs. Kaye, whom be had known for several years, was a very " hearty" woman. Mr. Cracroft : What do you mean by that ? idaitness : She was a strong, stout woman. Mr. Cracroft : We are told she was a very plucky woman ? Witness : So she was. Christopher Brown, landlord cf the Ram Inn. Arnold, spoke as to tW, prisoner being at that house on the even- ;ng of February 14. Accused left about twenty minutes past nine. Alfred Oliver, already referred to, corroborated the evidence of Mr. Powley as far as related to events at the Ram Inn, and identified prie.oner as the man who had a conversation' with Powlev on the inn steps. Whilst in the taproom prisoner asked witness who Mr.Powley was, and witness told him. Cross-examined There was a general talk about the local hoard eiection, and Powley was taking a leading part in it. Mr.Cracroft suggested that this was the reason for the pzisoner's question. William Turner, a frarnewnrk-knitter, living at Arnold stated that on the evening of February 14, about hale. past nine, a man greatly resembling the prisoner,though he would not swear to the identity, asked the way to Powley's house, and as he was not in the right way wit- ness went with him for some distance to the end of the footpath leading to Powley's. He accompanied him also about seven yards along the path, and then gave him the right direction and a caution to keep off the hedges. Cross-examined : He remembered telling the man he directed that it was a very dark night. Mr. Cracroft : What quarter was the moon in ? Witness (a little deaf) : Over the style to the right hand (great laughter). His Lordship, after consulting an almanac, said that he found there would be no moon that night. Re-examined, witness said it was light enough to see the cart road at the 'op of the footpath. Another framework-knitter named Marshall, who met the previous witness when with Wilkinson, identified the prisoner. • Mrs. Elizabeth Powley also identified the accused as the man who came to Kings Head Well on the 14th Feb-

div.head: PRESTON RAILWAY ACCIDENT.
div.p: THE PRESTON RAILWAY ACCIDENT.

AN IMPORTANT VERDICT. The coroner's jury which has inquired as.to the death of the young man Mayor, which was caused by the dis- aster to the Highland express at Preston, delivered an important verdict on Tuesday evening. After hearing evidence as to the hio speed at which expresses were driven through Preston station and over the sharp curve at the north end, a rate of speed maintained in defiance of the regulation that trains should not pass the curve at more than ten miles an hour, the jury found that the disaster was caused by "excessive high speed in travel- ling through Preston station." They did not consider that the two engine-drivers were alone to blame, the time allowed for the run between Wigan and Preston being too short; and they strongly recommended the London and North-Western Company to see that their by-laws were more strictly enforced.

div.head: SHIP CANAL
div.p: SHIP CANAL
LAST VGFEK'S TRAFFIC.

During the week ended July 17, the seagoing traffic on the canal was again much above the average,the arrivals being in fact the largest on record. The combined arrivals and sailings amounted to 191 vessels of 50733 net regis- tered tons, against 185 vessels of 47,323 tons in the pre- ceding week. Eleven vessels entered with timber from Canada and the Baltic, a full cargo of wheat—the first imported to Manchester from the Black Sea—arrived from Nicolaieff, three CAI goes of boulder flints from St. Valery, a cargo of ice from Christiania, and general car- goes from Australia, New York, Syria, Hungary, Ham- burg, R ,tterdam, Antwerp, Ghent, Beulogne, Treport, 11,4uen, and Paris. There were sailings to Genoa, Parie, Rouen, Treport, Boulogne, Ghent, Antwerp, Rotterdam, Hamburg, Sannesund, Gethenburg, Libau, Memel, Het- singfors, Archangel, and Trangesvaag (Faroe Islands), mlst of the vessels taking general cargo, coal, or salt. The coastwise traffic was of the usual character, the regular services to and from the principal home perts being responsible for the greater part of the tonnage. Forty-four head of cattle, 40 sheep,and six horses arrived frona Dublin by Friday's direct steamer. SIX MONTHS' TRADE.

For the third time in the last three months the Ship Canal has established a new record in the matter of traffic, and with all the summer trades now in full swing this steady progress may be expected to continue for several months. The remarkable increase in the June returns is, of course, mainly attributable to the timber traffic,and as this trade is already very much larger than it was a month ago.it may be confidently predicted that the July returns will considerably exceed the figures for June. Increases from month to month, however, afford a less conclusive proof of progress than comparisons of the corresponding periods of successive years. Accord- ingly we give the seagoing traffic for the first six months cf 1894, 1895, and 1896 respectively : Tons cargo. January 1 to June 30, 1894 January 1 to June 30, 1895 January 1 to June 30, 1898

The barge traffic and the revenue therefrom have also showu a steady though not an equally rapid growth. As comparisons are sometimes drawn between the Man- chester and Suez Canals, it is interesting to place side by side the results of half a year's working of each : January 1 to June 30, 1896.

Receipts. Ships. Net reg. tons. £ Manchester Ship Canal 3,832 ... 1.091,262 ... 78,564 Sur- z Canal .... 1.885 ... 4,592,171 ... 1,712,587 From this it appears that wnilst more than twice as many voyages were made along the Manchester water- way, the average siz,. of the vessels was only 285 tons net register. against 2,436 tons in the case of the Suez Canal. The receipts on the Manchester Canal average is. 6.1. per ten register, against 7s. 6J. per ton on the Su, z Canal. This difference is accentuated by the fact that nearly every steamer passes through the Suez Canal fully laden, whereas a large proportion of the vessels using the Ship Canal arrive or sail in ballast or only partly loaded. No ship dues being charged by the Manchester Canal Company, this can be done without extra cost to owners. The average earnings per ton on cargo passing through the Manchester Ship Canal in sea- going vessels was slightly under 2s. during the past half year, as against 24. 3-k l. per ton in the corresponding period of 1895 and 2,11 per ton in the first half of 1894. This would appear to indicate either that the lower- class traffic is increasing more rapidly that the higher class, or that the Company is giving shippers better terms in order to secure a larger volume of trade.

div.head: WARRINGTON MUNICIPAL FINANCE.
div.p: WARRINGTON MUNICIPAL FINANCE.
COUNCILLOR SAW GREEN IN REPLY.

AS the criticisms upon the finances of the Borough appeared to us deserving some reply at the hands of the Finance Committee, a reporter from this office waited upon the chairman and asked if lie had read the article.
" Yes" said he "And I very much regret that your correspondent made such a hurried examination of the accoun's or he would not have uttered such ar-
rant nonsense,aud it _would not have been necessary
o correct the error: he has macle.Were it not"a idea

the Councillor, "that you had introduced him as an expert financier, and as one who had had some ex- perience in municipal affairs and consequently that many people would naturally expect that what he said must be correct, I would have left the blunders to cure themselves, as they certainly would upon more thoughtful consideration" "Then would you prefer to let the matter rest?" "I would, but as I say,there are so many who can- not go into the circumstances for themselves and who would. take what they read after such a preface . . . . .
aa beyond doubt that,l think it better:to give all the information in my possession. It is not possible in a

budgetispeech to say all one would wish, and there- fore it may be interesting to the ratepayers to learn some other facts thatk those given upon pass- ing the minutes in the Council." "I am sure our readers will be very grateful for anything that will enlighten the ratepayers,' said our Correspondent, "for I have been told many times that finance is a difficult subject to grasp." " Well," said the Chairman, "your correspondent makes three general complaints, firstly, as to the manner in which the accounts are made up; secondly, that there has been a remarkable increase in the assessable value of the property in the borough and that it is in consequence of this increase that the rates have been reduced, and, thirdly, that by a consolidation of the indebtedness of the _borough a

saving of .0,000 a year could be effected. Taking them in this orcl,-.;r the first charge is that the annual report issued by the Treasurer is a confused state- ment of accounts. He then asks why the ratepayers cannot have a clear statement &c., and also why the assets of the borough are not set out? "Am I not correct in this ?" said the chairman. "So far as I can understand it, it is so."

"Now," said the chairman, "My reply to these charges is, first, that the accounts are kept so as to comply with the regulations of the Local Govern- ment Board and that to anyone who will take a little trouble they will be found clear, intelligible, and complete. Clear because there is in the first part from page 2to 17 a full account of all receipts and payments upon the borough rate, from page 20 to 43 a full note of all receipts and payments upon the improvement rate, from 46 to 61 full particulars of the general sewers rate and sundry special funds. These may be designated our cash accounts. We then have a clear and absolutely unimpeachable statement of the various debt redemption funds and the interest payable thereon,and then, after the gas and water accounts, we have, (so that everything may be seen at a glance), a summarised account of the whole. We then give a full statement of the debt of the borough ; and, lastly, we have a state- ment of all the bondholders the full list of which agrees accurately with the balance of the debt account. The accounts so clearly follow each other and so naturally that I may quote from another place and say that a wayfarer even if running might not only read but understand. I assert therefore, that instead of being confused it is particularly clear and plain andclutains the full- est possible information and 1 will go further and say that familiar as lam with most of the muni- cipal statements of the country, ours will be found to compare with any of them. We are not perfect but on the contrary we are always ready and will- ing to adopt any suggestion that is an improve- ment as anyone familiar with our accounts of six years ago will realize." "Now. Mr. Chairman, as to the list of assets what have you to say about that ? " "My answer is that it is not practicable and also that it is unnecessary. We give at the foot of page 155 a list of the chief assets. We have the gas and water works, park, market tolls, &c., all of which are continually diminishing values in the sense that the debts upon them are being reduced, but. w:iat about the cost of widen- ing streets, paving with sets old thfirou4hfares, purchase of easements, priviieges,the making of the public sewers, &c. flow are these to be valued? at original cost or present condition? and if they could of what service would it be? We are not a private firm that can group all its assets and bor- row upon them. We are not a trading concern that has to be balanced up to see if it is solvent and for which purpose a valuation of assets is ab- solutely necessary. Therefore I say it is unnecess- ary for it can serve no practical purpose. But for our own information and those of our successors all the particulars have in a large measure been worked out and put on record within a recent period." " Now,Mr. Chairman,what have you. to say about the increase of assessments ?"

"Simply that your correspondent evidently does I not realise what he is saying. There has been no 'remarkable' increase. Taking the years named by him,the difference is about .£lB,OOO Of this over £7,500 is the increase from newly erected property during the period, .£B.OOO comes from the inclusion of the Extension of 1890 within the Borough, £1,420 from increased assessments, and the balance trota a few spscial circumstances. The value of the Extension had been all discounted before it came into possession for it brought with it a natural annual charge.' "What have you to say to our correspondent's statement that the increase of assessments is equal to a saving of 8,1. in the £? " "That it is a most absurd statement and you can test it in a moment. Assume that it was possible to levy a rate at ss. Bd. in the X -Ton this £lB,OOO it would certainly produce as stated 81. in the Xor say £5,000, but then you must know the main part is cottage property subject to a special composition and another large part is arable land chargealole at + only. The Bd. therefore is thus seriously reduced. Having shown the impossibility ,of getting Bd. in the X out of the increase let me show you another aspect of the subject, that we as a committee have to take into account, viz., the in- crease of our expenditure which as the following figures will show has much to do with the matter. In 1893 with 81. in the .£ towards the smallpox debt our expendituie was £40,174 whilst for the year 1896 our expenditure is no less than £38,926. Yet in spite of this we have reduced the rate from 3s. Bd. in 1893 to 21. 8. in 1896, I am satisfied to leave it to the ratepayers as to whethe, this reduction has been brought about by the Assessment C•mtimittee or by the care and skill of the Finance Committee. We are only mortal and we 01 ay make mistakes. We do not make the cir- cumstances, but we claim to have done the best that. could he done under those circumstances.'
" What have you now to say to the consolidation of the debts ?,"

"Again I must protest against the assumption of your correspondent, but I will show you how groundless is his attack. We have a great number of loans upon various amounts, and these are to be repaid in varying periods. Now your correspondent suggests that we should consolidate i.e. group all these together and get an Act to extend the period of repayment. Your correspondent in this overlooks the fact that the lynx eye of the Local government Board is al- ways watching Corporation finance, and any such attempt would he opposed by them, and I may, therefore, say it would not be allowed. The law is that all capital monies are to be repaid so that future generations may not be improperly taxed. and according to the nature of the intended expendi- ture the term within which it must be repaid is fixed. Now suppo,.e we could do what your cor- , respon lent sugges's it might be so manipulated that. the loans would never be repaid. To a very slight extent we were permitted to do this in our Gas Act. We suggested a similar scheme to the Local novernment Board about fifteen months ago, and we were told we might conAolidate 'pen the average period the loans had to run if we would iesue stock. We went thoroughly into the matter and we found it would not be wise, and certainly would not save u 4 anything in comparison with the cost and trouble. The suggested saving of £3OOO a year is not possible? I have just said it would not save us any thing. It could only be done on the avera(re and that too on the issue of a stock. Thi- latter course has its advantages, but it has als, great disadvantages, and in our judgment we hate done much better. We have not a loan at a highs irate than three per cent., whilst we have succeede in getting all we have recently required and that a very large rmount ut 21, and 1

venture to say from what 1 learned at Brighton that some of our municipalities -who have issued stork very much envy UR. I shall' be.more than sati-:4ld if your readers from this get a better ac- quaintance with our finances, not a very eritertain- ing sufij,ct at the hest, . but I ; should be better pleased still it your correspondent would place his undoubted ability at the service of the ratepayers an 4 help those of I.F; who are doing our best instead of making these extravagent charges through the columns of a paper.

div.head: ALLEGED THEFT FROM A GOLBORNE MAN.
div.p: ALLEGED THEFT FROM A GOLBORNE MAN.

At the Warrington Occasional Court on Monday, before Mr. Ziba Armitage, William Edit rsley was charged with stealing two silver lever watches, valued at £6, the property of William Dickenson, Golborne, on the 14th inst.—William Dickenson, in his defence, said that he lived at 2; Brook-street, Golborne,and on the 14th inst., about 230,4 e was in a public-house in Golhorne along with the prisoner and went from the public-hcthe to a reservoir near the Claiborne collieries for the purpose of having a bathe. He gave the watch to the prisoner to hold while he went into the water,.and on returning ha found the prisoner had decamped. He had not seen him since. One of the watches produced was iden- tified as his (witness's) property. The other watch had not been recovered.—Sergeant [lege deposed to apprehending prisoner at Billinge on Saturday night.—Prisoner was remanded to the Newton Sessions.

IN an address which he gave to the The Navy, Liverpool Chamber of Commerce at the beginning of the week, Lord CHARLES BERESFORD made some very important and indeed rather startling statements. During the last few years there has been a great deal said about the navy and largo sums of money have been voted by Parliament for the purpose of strengthening the naval defences of the country. But, according to Sir CHARLES BERESFORD, there is still a weak link, and unfortunately in this case the weakest link is the most imprtaint one. We have, it appears, got the ships—or at all evants we shall have them as soon as the present building programme is completed—and we have got the money, but we haven't get the men. Even to man the ships which are either ready for use or are rapidly approaching completion in the ship- yards the country is short of no less than 28,000 men. The Government are now buildang forty-six new ships, yet are, it is said, not taking steps to provide any additional sailors. If this be the case, Lord CHARLES BERESFORD may well say that if business men ran their trades as the navy is conducted they would be bankrupt in six months. There is, of course, a comfortable feeling abroad that all de- fizieneies in the Royal Nava!,would in time of war be speedily rectified by drawing upon the mer- cantile service, which, it is popularly believed, would yield a practically exhaustless supply of well-qualified mariners. But this is evidently a delusion. In these days of highly scientific war- fare a man-of-wars man to be of much use needs a very special training. He cannot, in the opinion of Sir CHARLES BERESFORD, be given this training in a period of less than five years. Naval warfare is now a much more complex affair than it was in the days of Nelson. At the beginning of the cen- tury a sailor from a merchant ship could within a few days almost be transformed into a very effi- cient " sea-clog," but that cannot be done now. In the second place the manning of the Navy from the mercantile marine is becoming more diffiult by reason of the fact that English sailors are being rapidly ousted from English merchant ships by foreigners. No fewer than forty per cent of the seamen in the British mercantile marine are of foreign extraction. Those men, it is evident, cannot be relied upon to fight for this country in the event of a great war ; in fact a large pro- portion of them might go over to the hostile fleet. Shipowners no doubt find it is eJon mnical to em- ploy foreigners on their vessels, but when looked at from a national point of view, this discourage- ment of British seamanship is a very serious mat- ter. Under the whole of the circumstances, Lord CHARLES BERESFORD makes out a very good case for the establishment of a naval reserve.

The members of this club made an excursion to the estuary of the Mersey between Hale and Speke on Saturday. Travelling by rail to 'ialewood the .party walk.ed thence to the Dungeon Near this point was the stranded steamer Palmyra. Mr. P. Monks had kindly arranged for tea being supplied in the saloon of this vessel,the"list"on wnich was so great as to make even the most broad-minded mem- bers take a one sided view of things. The afternoon and evening were somewhat too cloudy for fly or moth-hunting. but the botanists were very success- fail, ,Whilst those who study spiders or beetles were not lessso. Of spiders the fine agelena labyrinthica was 91fmtiful, and the rare epeira patagiata was also taken.
