div.head: EXAMINER SATURPAY, JULY 25, 1896.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURPAY, JULY 25, 1896.

A CARNIVAL NIGHT AT RUNCORN. SUCCESSFUL CYCLE PARADE. Wednesday, the day appointed for the holding by the Runcorn Cycle Club, of a flower carnival and lantern parade, dawned somewhat dull and gusty, but towards the evening the atmospheric conditions underwent a de- cided improvement, and at the time of the starting of the parade the weather was all that could be desired. Perhaps it is somewhat late in the day to state the object of the festivity, but the object a good one), will bear reretition. The club has opened at Parr's Bank, a Cot- tage Hospital Fund, into which the proceeds of the par- ade, together with other subscriptions, donations, and collections as may accrue will be paid. To give the fund a substantial governing body, three trustees Messrs. S. Taylor, J.P., C.C., E. Imison, C.C., and H. Wright,have been appointed.and the money gathered or raised will re- main at the bankers until such tune as it is thought suffi- cient funds have been collected to warrant the formation of a committee to carry on the work of procuring and managing a hospital. Everyone,since the idea was first mooted, has favourably received the scheme, and Sir J. Brunner in sending a donation of £lO as a" small but practical proof of his sympathy expressed the pleasure with which he had heard of the under- taking,which he hoped would be crowned with success." This hope echoed in the hearts and minds of the club, the committee and the officials appointed to carry out the work, many of whom have been untiring in their efforts, to bring the carnival to a successful termination. Special credit in organising the undertaking, well earned, and entirely due,should be given Mr. W. H. Mack the bard working secretary, Messrs. W. E. Dudley and W. Grounds his assistant I secretaries and Mr. H. Wright, the treasurer; while the committee also deserve unstinted praise, as they have sacrificed time and gone to con- siderable trouble in attending and doing the work of the committee. But to the procession itself. The secre- taries' invitations scattered broadcast over the local cycling world brought ready responses, and there was no lack either of processionista or collectors. Wednesday evening saw the front of the secretaries' office thronged with arrivals, and collectors besieged Mr. Wright, the treasurer, who was distributing. boxes and badges. People were beginning to gather in the centre of the town and Devonshire Square the marshalling resort of the first section wore quite an animated appearance. So also did High-st. the resort of No. 2 section, and Bridge- water-st. the resort of No. 3 and the end of Bridgewater- at. the headquarters of No. 4. At each of these points were, individually, Mr. W. E. Dudley, Messrs. Stubbs and Rushton, Messrs. A. Grounds, and W. Grounds, and Mr. H. Branch who had an anxious and exciting time in getting the processionists into something like order. About seven o'clock the three sections were got to- gether and began to move down the prescribed route in good order. The processionists were indeed a motley crowd. Every conceivable sueject was either represented or caricatured. King Lear stalked magestically through the streets armed with a colkcting box closely pursued by a bridal party, the male in the coventional frock coat, and the happy lady in the yet unconventional bloomers. Of "new women" in that costume there were several. There was a gentleman who walked along dis- guised as a beer barrel which costume secured a prize. There were soldiers, sailors, policemen, bakers, clowns, gypsies, foreign noblemen and tramps mixed up in de- lightful confusion. Then there were the gaily dressed cycles and many happy and orginal ideas were exploited. The ladies were attired in the wonderful dress to repre- sent characters both ancient and modern. Their machines were draped with flowers, ribbons, ice., and Jewel- ese lanterns were hung on every angle or projection on which anything could be fastened. Mephistepholes mounted on a donkey drawing a tricycle bearing Weary Willie and Wandering Waggles was labelled, "going home," and caused much amusement. The tradesmen were represented by brilliantly dressed turnouts* Amongst the trades represented being—printing, coal, grocery, clothing and dry soap, all known by some exhibitel feature of the business. The effi.oial order of the procession was as follows :- 1. Bugle Band 2nd (BC.) V. B. Cheshire Regiment. Marshalls—Weary Willie and Wandering Waggles, a in tandem, Runcorn Lady Wheelers. Band of the 2ed (8.C.) VB. Cheshire Regiment. Cycling Section, Army Corps, Orford Btrrarke, Sr. John Ambulance Associa- tion, Runcorn Fire Brigade, Helsby Fire Brigade and Band. 2. Runcorn Cycle Club, Runcoru Town Band, Wid- nes, C.C., Hough Green C.C., Lostook Alkali C.C., Weston Cnurch Band, Northwich C.C., Liverpool Licensed Victuallers' C.C., Chester C.C., members of C.T.C. and others. 3. Weston Wesleyan Band. Members of the Run- corn Football Club, with the Lancashire Challenge Cup, Tableau by Weston Church Scholars—" Queen and Attendants." Nelson-street Subscription Band. div.head: RUNCORN ANT) WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN ANT) WIDNES.
RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.
This Court was held on Tuesday, uut there were no eases of public interest. RETURN OF THE VICAR OF RUNCORN.

Last Saturday the Rev. Canon Maitland Wood re- turned to Runcorn after a protracted holiday, in search of health. The rev, gentleman took part in the service on Sunday. In honour of the home coming the bells pealed vigorously on Saturday in the Parish Church. RD'NCORK PARISH CHURCH.

The annual sermons on behalf of the diocese were preached in this church on Sunday. The preachers were the Rev. W. Hodvon,M.A..,vicar of Widnes in the Worn- ing,and the Rev. A. Symons. M.A., of Stockport, in the evening. Good congregations assembled and the ser- vices were rendered additionally interesting by the ap- propriate music rendered by the choir. The collections realized about £l5. RIWARD IOR BRAVERY AT RUNCORN.

The Liverpool Shipwreck and Humane Society have awarded George Pickstock, of 29, Wellington-st., Run- corn, £1 for gallant conduct. Our readers will probably remember that on the 25'h of June, Pickstock was standing on the canal side at Top Locks, High-st., when a child named Harry Moores, of Ha.ndley-st., fell into the water. The child was in great danger, and went down twice when Pickstock with conspicuous bravery, jumped into the water and brought the youngster to sqe to the side. What makes Mr. Pickstock's action more commendable is the fact that he was just recover- ing from an attack of sciatica, and was at the time off work, and as a result of the cold plunge he was confined to bed for a week. Superintendent Okell placed the facts of the case before the Society, with a result that Sergeant Gill was able to hand to the rescuer on behalf of the Society, a small acknowledgemnt of his brave conduct. The recipient has been instrumental in saving three other lives from drowning. RUNCORN FRER LIBRARY COMMITTER. The monthly meeting of this committee was held in the Town Hall. Runcorn, on Tuesday night. Present— Messrs. W. Hancll,,r (in the chair), H. J. Grice, W. J. Cunningham, Dr. Gas'aldi, and.). D. Jones (librarian). div.p: WARRINGTON BA3K it UP ICY COURT.

FRlDAY.—Before Mr. Registrar Ridgway. FAILURE OF A RUNCORN HARDWARE DEALER AND CON. FEcrioNNß.—Joseph Tickle. now of 5, Alcock-street, Runcorn, and carrying on business at the Market Hall, Runcorn as a hardware dealer and confectioner, but lately residing and carrying on business at 17, Bridge- street and previously at 31. and 33,E4erton-street,Runcorn came up for his first publie exainination in bankruptcy. The gross liabilities were £149 4s. al.. and the assets £3B 18s. 2d., leaving a deficiency of £llO 61. The bank- rupt stated he: had been in business as a hardware dealer, and confec.tioner, at various ad;iresses in Run- corn, for about fivt. years, having commenced without capital. While carrying on such business, he had worked.as a journeym. n tailor. He had not kept any books of account; and was unable to explain how his deficiency had arisen, except as to £47, estimated loss on rsnlizition of his assets. Be first knew of his insol- vency abiut six months aeo ; and had with such know- ledge contracted a few debts,during the past six months, which were still owing. The unsecured liabilities were almost wholly trade liabilities. The security in the hands of the fully secured creditor was a policy of the Prudential Assurance Company. for £lOO, payable in or about 1910, or at the bankrupt's prior decease. The bankrupt's wife claimed the household f urni- tine on the ground that it was hers prior to the marriage, w• ich took place on the 14th of June, 1888. The bankrupt alleg,od that he sold his own furniture to enable him to file his petition. He stated that the causes of the failure were bad trade and loss by fires. Trade had been very bad in Runcorn ever since the coal strike. The chemical trade was very had there. He was not ea nable of keeping proper ac- counts. The Assistant Officio.' R .epiver said the exa- mination might be closed. He had great sympathy with the debtor.

div.head: INTERESTING WEDDING AT RUNCORN.
div.p: INTERESTING WEDDING AT RUNCORN.

On Tuesday at two o'clock an interesting wedding took place at the Runcorn Parish Church, the contract- ing parties being Mr. James B. Holland, well-known as the manager of the Runcorn and Frodsham branch of Parr's Bank,son of Mr. D. Holland,of Knutsford,aud Miss Mazy G.Bankes,eldest daughter of the late Mr.W.Bankes of Weston. The charch was thronged with friends of the bride and bridegroom,the ceremony being performed by the Rev. Canon Wood assisted by the Rev. H. B. Firth. The bride was given away by her uncle, Mr. Bankes, of Over Hall. The best man was Mr. W. B. Frith, and the other groomsman being Mr. Stanley Bankes. The bridesmaids were the Misses Ernmie and Daisy Bankes, sisters of the bride. The bride wore a dress of white ivory satin with bodice covered with chiffon and trimmed with pearl passementerie with a tulle veil and a wreath of orange blossoms. The chiffon and blossoms were fastened on the veil and train. She wore a diamond ring and ried a shower bouquet of stephanotis,roses,and white heather. Miss E. Bankes wore a fancy white alpaca frock trimmed with silk and chiffon, and Miss Daisy Bankea wore a cream satin liberty frock trimmed with pink and chiffon. They also wore fancy straw hats with white ostrich tips and carried bouquets of pink roses. Mrs. Bankes wore a handsome gown of coloured silk trimmed with white silk chiffon and spangles and carried a bouquet of red roses. The bridal party were conveyed to the church in six coaches, Subsequently the newly married couple left for the honeymoon which will be spent in Scotland and Ireland, the bride's going away dress being blue gray cloth, white and gold waistcoat, lined with sh)t silk and white reefer, with chip ha:. Amongst many presents was a silver salver bearing the inscription" Presented to Bro. J. B. Holland, P.M., by the W.M. and brethren of the Cholmondelev Lodge of Ancient and Accepted Free- masons, No. 1908, on the occasion of his wedding. Frodsham, July 21, 1896."

div.head: TILE NUISANCE AT WILDERSPOOL.
div.p: TILE NUISANCE AT WILDERSPOOL.

Mr. Reginald Pacts, clerk to the Cheshire County Council, forwarded copies of a resolution passed by the Parish Council of Grappenball in reference to a nuisance arising from the state and the condition of the water in the disused portion of the River Mersey at Apple- ton, near Warrington. The resolution read "That a memorial be forwarded to the Rivor's Pollution Commit- tee of the Cheshire County Council complaining of the foul smells from tha Ship Canal and the old river near Wilderspool and urging that steps be taken to ascertain to wt om the responsibility attaches and whether any remedial measures can be taken to obviate the nuisance which may involve very serious consequ- ences, and which is already causing sickness as well as much discomfort and annoyance throughout the district which it affects.—alr. Ashton said he replied to Mr. Potts stating that the Warrington Corporation were con- structing a sewer and had pas=ed contracts for the work. He received next day a reply from Mr. Potts stating that the Town Clerk of Warrington had communicated with him stating that the Council had at the meeting on Tuesday passed a contract for the construction of the sewer.

div.head: SHIP CANAL AND THILIOHTING OF BRIDGES.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL AND THILIOHTING OF BRIDGES.

A letter was read from Mr.-W. H. Hunter, engineer to the Ship Canal Campany stating that the Company was under an obligation to light such bridges over the canal as were constructed under the Act of 1885 ; but the Council would find that certain bridges authorised by the Act were abandoned under the Various Powers Act 1890, and that certain other bridges were authorised by the Act of 1890 in regard to which the Company had no obligation so far as lighting was concerned.—The Coun- cil contended that the Ship Canal Company were liable. DANGEROUS CONDITION OF LATCHFORD LOCKS. In regard to the footbridge across Latchford Locks,Mr. Hunter on behalf of the Ship Canal wrote that he did not understand what the Clerk to Grappenhall Parish Council meant by " protecting the Latchford Locks " and would be glad if the Rural Council would inform him, The footways across the canal were effectually protected by hand rails, and he was not aware of any provision in the Act of Parliament or agreement under which the Company could be called upin to provide for the lighting of the, locks or footway.—The Surveyor pointed out that the bridges were railed hut there was no protection from the side of the canal.—Mr. Heywood: The Company are going to do everything that the Act provides but nothing mare.--The Clerk was ordered t.) press the matter fot ward.

A GRIEVANCE OF THE LIDIES' COMMITTEE.

He moved that a letter be sent to the Ladies' Committee saving they were sorry that the remark had been made.—Mr. Heywood pointed out that the question, indeed,the letter itself wnis read in a somewhat frivolous manner audithe Words he made use of were simply spoken in jest. At the same time the ladies had put forward the same day a request that they might be allowed to visit the male side of the house,and the theught struck him at once that this might be a good commencement for the ladies to use that jedg- ment they were so noted for with regari to the male side of the house, and he suggested th nrel entirely in a frivolous manner. At the same tim- there were times when the reporters were only too glad to out their small jokes into print rather than some of their rmkre import- ant business. div.head: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

On Wednesday,the monthly meeting of this Board was held in the Boardroom at the Workhouse. The chair was occupied by Mr. S. Davias,and there were also pre- sent Mrs. Clay, Rev. J. H. Riddette, Dr. Patterson, Messrs. G. Pilling, J. W. Knowles, A. J. Jolley, William Houghton, J. Dignum, William Hickman, J. Clarke, J. Houghton,W. Cross, T. Malkin, J. Billinge, T. Halton,J. Ball,J. Warburton, A. Jolley, E. L. B9nt, J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (deputy clerk), C. H. Ward (master), and H. M. Mines (superintendent of Padgate schools).
HOUSE COMMITTEE.

This committee at its meeting on the 10th July hav- ing received the resignation of Nurse Carter recom- mended that the same be accepted,and that her request for a testimonial as to the satisfactory discharge of her duties be acceeded to. It was also recommended that the tender of Mr. S. Moss for the supply of an unclimb- able fence at 6s. J. per yard be accepted.—The min- utes were passed on the motion of M. A. J. Jolley, se- conded by Mr. A. Jolley.

div.head: MISCONDUCT OF THE INMATES ON WALKING DAY.
div.p: MISCONDUCT OF THE INMATES ON WALKING DAY.

The Workhouse Master, in his journal, reported that the privilege of allowing the inmates a holiday on Walk- ing Day, was very much abused, many coming home in a drunkenntate and making a great disturbance so much so that they had to call in the police at midnight. Some of the inmates did not return until next morning, and he hoped the Board would withhold the privilege in the future.—The Chairman said he would be sorry to see the inmates deprived from seeing the sights of Walking Day.—Mr. A. J. Jolley said the matter was carefully con- sidered by the committee,and it was felt that to deprive the decent portion of the inmates the annual holiday be- cause some individuals had misconducted themselves, would be harsh and unfair. It was decided that the Master should keep a recprd of inmates who miscon- ducted themselves, and that these in future be debarred , from leaving on such occasions.—Mr. John Houghton , said that was the best way to deal with the matter.— The Committee's action was approved.

div.head: NEW INFIRMARY.
div.p: THE NEW INFIRMARY.

The minutes of the Infirmary Committee stated that Mr. Owen explained his procedure with reference to the proposed infirmary, and exhibited a type plan for an infirmary with 200 beds and suggested several matters upon which he de ired the views of the Committee. The Committee had, therefore, considered the matter and made several suggestions. It was decided that the new infirmary shall be erected upon the new plot of land agreed to be purchased having an area of five acres, three roods, nine perches, and that the entrance to the infirmary from the outside shall be through the grounds of the present workhouse and not from the side street opening into Lovely-lane.—Mr. Owen stated that Mr. G. Smith had advised him to inspect the Dewsbury work- house infirmary as being on the best lines f3r an in- firmary of the size required, and he purposed doing so at his own expense but it was desirablethe Clerk should arrange for the inspection with the clerk of the Dew- bury Union and that he should accompany him on the visit. The Committee concurred and instructed the Clerk accordingly. The plans would be submitted to the Board for their full consideration before submission to the Local Government Board.—The minutes were confirmed on the motion of Mr. Houghton, seconded by , Mr. Pilling.
THE LATCHFORD REGISTRATION DISTRICT.

A letter was read from the Registrar General acknow- ledging the Board's reply to his communication, stating that after very careful examination of the enumeration books it secmed that at the census in 1891 only 2,545 persons resided %Rhin the area to be shortly added to the birough of Warrington, which together with the population enumerated within the existing borough made the population of the extended borough in 1891, 55,288. It was therefore evident to the Registrar General that neither as regarded area nor population would the enlarged borough be beyond the capacity of a single registrar. Unless Latchford be added to War- rington sub-district, the part of Winwick civil parish could not be transferred to Winwick sub-district, with- out compensation being plid to the Warrington regis- trar for loss of fees. The Registrar General under the circumstances found himself unable to accede to the Guardian's reque,t that Latchford might remain a separate sub-district, &though its amalgamation with Warrington sub-district need not take plsce until the ex- tension of the boroo2h took effect.—The Clerk stated that the matter rested with the Registrar General and it was no use kicking against the pricks.

div.head: NON-PAUPER SCHOOL FEES.
div.p: NON-PAUPER SCHOOL FEES.

The Local Government Board wrote with reference to the re-appointment of Mr. B pive, as enquiry offic,:r, stating that the Board desired to be informed of the number of applications which the Guardians had re- ceived for filo payment of non-pauper school fees.during the years 294-5 6.—Mr. Bowes,who was called into the room ,stateu that there had been none.—Tne Clerk sta'ed that when Mr. Bows was appointed, it was deAded that he should hav€ a salary of £lOO. £95 was given him for his work as enquiry officer, and £5 for any work in c.onnection with school fees for non-pauper school children. He supposed that the Board would be willing to place the salary of enquiry officer at £lOO per annum in the event of the latter office becoming de- funct.—Approval was expressed of this course being taken.

div.head: CHILDREN AT PIDGATE SCHOOLS.
div.p: THE CHILDREN AT PIDGATE SCHOOLS.
The CHAIRMAN sAiel there were tow 139 children in the; schools. They had had as many as 203 in at once, and he thought the present low nunatwr spoke well for the condition el the town.
THF, REPRESENTATION' OF LITTLE SANKEY.-TOWS V.
COUNTRY OUARDIANS.

In accordance with notice given, Mr. PILLING moved that application be made to the County Council for an additional guardian for that part of St. Austin's ward included in the extended portion of the borough, and formerly Little Sankey. In doing so he pointed out that it was only right that Little Sankey which was at pre- sent represented as a district, and had now been in- cluded in the borough should have a representative guardian. It was the duty of • the Board to assist the . electors by asking permission from the County Council to have a guardian for that portion.—Mrs. Clay se- conded the resolution.—Mr. William Houghton said Burtonwood was entitled to another ra presentative. It was a very large township and had not fair representa- tion on that Board. The guardians representing the borough had a great advantage °vele those in the out- lying districts. They ware able to get to the Boardroom in a few minutes whereas it was very difficult ler coun- try guardians to attend the meeting. He did not ob- ject to the prrsent application but he thought Burton- wood was entitled to another guar fian.—Mr Keowles . opposed the resolution, and thought that a small town- ship like Little Sankey might be swallawed up by the borough without asking the County C nuncil for a repre- sentative for it. No one could say but that the borough was ably, eloquently, and influentially represented .on that Board. (Leuehter.) The Guardians of outlying districts were obliged to lose half a day or a day in order to attend the meetings and the borough members had a great advantage in that respect.—Mr. A. J. Jolley said the only. argument adduced in favour of the application was that there would be a large number of people on whom injustice weuld be inflicted unless a Guardian was obtained. But already there was a great injustice to the inhabitants of Warrington for they were grossly unrepresented, and be (Mr. Jolley) was like one crying in the wilderness in protesting aeainst thie injustice at the time of the re-arrangement. He would move an amendment that application be made to the Lancashire Ceunty Council for a rtpresentative for each of the nine wards of the borough. 'They would then be going on right lines. To ask for an additional representa- tive for 2.000 people seemed absurd.—The Rev. J. H. Riddette said it was hardly a question of 2,000 People being represented. They were already represented on the Board of Guardians and he did not think the inhab- itants of Little Sankey should lose that representation because they had been included in the Borough of War rington.—The Clerk said tlarre was only one question before the Boerd and that was an application for an additional guardian for the borough. The proposal oh Mr. Jolley would come in conflict with the opinions held by the County Council. They would not split the b.irough into wards as proposed.—Mr. A. J. Jolley said that was a matter on which they were to form an opin ion. Tee County Council had treated the borough with ereat iejuatice but that was no reason why tney should si• , down and abide by it.—Mr. Halton seconded Mr. Jolley' • amendment.— The Clerk stated that the B arough had been incorporated for 50 years and yet it censisted of tI4, same number of councillors. ,The Board of Guardia; had increased its members. It the nernber wae to b. still further increased there weuld he 50 or 60 guardians sitting in that room. He would ask what the practica effect would b ? Would any ward be better retireeentee t or have greater kfluence ? Tine amendment of Mr. I Jolley's was out of order and was in opposition to tin- views of the County Council on the metter,—Mr. W;:- Hem flouehton asked the mover of the resolutien if he I weeld postpone it until the next* meeting.—Mr. Pihlia nenje he lead given a m intles net;ce, and wished the mat- ter to be decided up m that morning.—Mr. Keowles sods'. he uelerstood that if the County Council acceded to the applieetion,St.Austin's ward would have two representa- twee on the Board. It was most. improper.—Ttie Clcrk said ti.at was the result of the extension of tine Borough. The Corporation ought to make the wards more equal—The Chairman said considering the large popu- lation of Little Sankey it would he unfair and take their representative from them .—Mr. Warbu rton spoke in favour of Burtonwood having two represente- nves.—Ou a vote being taken, ten voted for the motion and ten against.—The Chairman gave his casting veto in favour of the motion.-Ir. Knowles then propose that the application be postponed for a month.—Mr. Hickman said the motion had been passed and it ceele not be rescinded without notice of motion.— Var. I Knowles said he woula give notice that he would meye that the motion be reacinded.—Mr. Hickman : i be vexed if you cannot have it all your own way.—Mr. Knowles. I am not vexed, but [will give notice now, I —The Clerk hoped that the members would not put him in tlaeiposition of applying to the County Council, and t then to pass something to the contrary. He thought it vnenuld be better to leave any ether application over until 1 the members' period of office had exp;red.—Mr. Knowles asked the Clerk to inform the County Council that the

motion was won by the casting vote of the Chairman. The motion had been carried by the town guardians.— The Clerk said he would leave it to the gentlemen who objected to send their own opinions, lie should give the voice of the majority not of the minority.—Mr. Hickman.: We don't want to be more ridiculous than we are. (Laughter.)—The suhjoct then dropped.
SUPERANNUATION OP MR. MINES.

The CHAIRMAN moved the following resolutions "That hi consideration of the twenty eight and a half ye‘r's service in this Union of Mr. Henry Montagu Mines,and of his state of health as certified by Dr.Josepb, a euwrannuation allowaace be awarded to him and that the value of all the emoluments of his several offices be included in the calculation of the amount of such allow- • ance ; that the total annual value of his salary and emoluments being estimated to be £l6l the superannua- tion allowance to be granted to him be at the rate of one sixtieth part thereof, in respect of each of his 28-1 years of service; that the superannuation allowance be accordingly fixed at the annual sum of £76 93. 63., com- mencing fvm the date of the determination of his service in his present offices subject to approval thereof by the Local Government Board." The Rev. J. H. Riddette seconded.—Mr. Cross asked whether there was a sp,-cial fund to pay the superan- nuation ?—The Clerk said there was a Bill before Parlia- ment waiting the third reading whereby a fund could be raised for this purpose. At present the charge fell upon the rates, but it Was understood by the officers that they were entitled to superannuation.—Mr. Cross said he asked the question at a previous meeting whether the new officers understood that they were going to have a pension, but he did not receive a direct answer. It now appeared that they were of the opinion that they would receive a pension.—The Rev. J. H. Riddette said as men of honour they were bound to carry out the arrange- ment with Mr. Mines.—Mr. Jolley asked that the names of those who voted should be recorded. On being put to the vote, 17 supported the resolution and three voted against, viz. :—Mrs. Clay, Mr. A. J. Jolley, and Mr. Clarke. This concluded the business.

div.head: MOST READERS
div.p: MOST READERS

Have had some experience of sick rooms, either as patients or attendants. How many such are there who have not felt the weakness or debility which follows the sickness, more discouraging than even the weakness it- self? Though the disease may have given way before the timely application of proper remedies, and though.in cinte-quence, no immediate danger is to be apprehended, the slow progress towards convalescence is very dis- heartening to patient and attendant alike. Hew often do we hear people say :—" Yes. 'The fever has left him. He is free from any immediate danger. But ho is so weak. If only he could regain strength " This debilitating effect of fever and other diseases is indeed a great source of anxiety to medical men as well as to their patients; and anything which would tend directly to shorten the period between the departure of the fever and the complete recovery of strength would be naturally welcomed by both doctors and patients. , This is one of the mast:vas why Gwilym Evans' Qtrinine Bitters is so popular, why doctors prescribe it so largely, why chemists sell it so generally, why patients have re- course to it so readily, and why everybody has a good word to say for it. Not only does it attack the disease in its stronghold, not only does it drive the evil from the system, but it gives back directly the strength of which the system has been deprived by illness; it infuses new life into the blood, and the recovery of. health and strength, instead of being, as it otherwise would be, dis- couragingly slow, intermittent, and uncertain, becomes, when this excellent medicine is resorted to„encouragingly rapid, regular, and certain. It is therefore confidently recommended as an unrivalled tonic medicine, and may be safely used by all who suffer from any form of weak- ness or debility from whatever cause it may arise.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
SIX MONTHS' HARD LABOUR TOR A MILITIAMAN.

Before the Magistrates at the Warrington Borough I Police Court on Wednesday morning,a young militiaman named Joseph Hartshorne was charged with committing an aggravated assault en Sarah King, whilst in a brick- field off Orford-lane at midnight on Tuesday.—Defend- ant pleaded not guilty.—The Chief Constable said this was a very bad case indeed and ene in which, he sub- mitted,the full penalty of the law should be visited upon defendant. The circumstances were tnat an old lady, Sarah King, 63 years of age, at - quarter to twelve midnight on Tuesday was going from her residence 7, Morris'-yard, off Silver-stret to her daughter's house in Watkin-street and she had to cross some waste ground off Orford-street. Whilst the e she eneountered the de- fendant. The latter spoke insultingly to her and she hurried on. She had not gone far before she felt herself seiz•sl and thrown to the ground by defendant. He at- tempted to assault her and she screamed"murder." P.C. Bell was near and heard complainant. He ran to the spot and prisoner bolted but left his cap on the ground ith his regimental number in it. Bell picked the old woman up and afterwards met the prisoner without cap. He askel him where it was and prisoner was confused and said he had lost it in a fight in town. Bell took him into custody and he was identified by the woman. Th- number in the cap also corresponded with the number on the defendant's clothing.—Mrs. King, a widow, corroborated the Chief ' Constable.—P.C. Bell also 'supported the 4taternefit and I said that Wilf0:1 he ran up he turned his bull's eye on de- fendant and saw the cap on the filor. He met him half- an•hour later, and questioned him as stated.—Defendant averred that he was innocent and that he had lost his cap in a cult..—The bench however sentenced him to the maximum penalty,six months' hard labour.
A PAINFUL CASE.-.43AERNTS GIVE EVIDENCE A.GLINST
THEIR SON

Bafore the magistrates at the Warrington Borough Court on Monday, John William Travis, a well-known character to the police, was charged with stealing from the dwelling-house of his father,George Travis, Winwick- road, a man's shirt, value 25., and further charged with stealing from the same place between the 19th and 21st, a man's vest, a pair of boots and a lady's black bodice, value 20s.—The Chief Constable informed the magis- trates that the charge had been reduced from one of burglary to larceny in order that the prisoner, who had been remanded for a week, might be dealt with at that court. The Chief Constable proceeded to state the facts concerning the fir t charge which hay. already been published, showing that the prisoner was seen by his parents in the act of poking a prop through the back kitchen window at about 4.30 in the morning. He dis- appeared over the wall and the shirt was afterwards missed. The palice had been unable to recover it. The prisoner had been allowed by his mother to visit the house on several occaaions and certain articles were missed between April 19-h end 22nd. The articles men- tioned in the charge had been pawned in various places and traced directly to the prisoner. One boy was present to whom he gave the boots in Widnes for the purpose of timing them pawned. He told the boy that they be- longed to his wife who was very ill. As a matter of fact the prisoner had not a wife. Shortly afterwards, the prisoner went to his aunt and gave her the pawn tickets of the stolen property stating that he would release the articles when he got work. That was clearly an admission that he stole them —Mrs. Travis, mother of the prisoner, residing at 53, Winwick- road, who was much affected in court, stated that she saw her son with he prop through the scullery window, She could not do any good with him. He had been in the habit of stealing things from her.—George Travis. father of the prisoner, also gave evidence.—P.C. Monks stated that he apprehended the prisoner, and on being r charged with the theft of the shirt he replied "I couldn't reach the shirt, I didn't take it."—Mary Travis, recalled, stated that. her sister gave her some pawn tickets, and she went to Widnes and released some pre- perty from several pawnshops there. The articles pro- duced had been pawned in different names.—Alice Knight, 38, Winwick-road, aunt to the prisoner, stated that he came to her house and asked her to take charge of the pawn tickets. She asked him what he had taken the things for, and he replied that he did not know.—James McCarthy, 13 veers of age, living at 14. Oxford-st, Widres, stated that the prisoner came up to him in Widnes and asked him to pawn the boots pro- duced. He told witness that he lived in Snif,7-lane, Widnes.—Detective-S Tveant Monaghan stated- that he received a pawn ticket from the prisoner's aunt, and on Tuesday he went to Liverpool and received the bodice produced. It had been pawned in Griat Crosshall-st. The prisoner on being asked whether he had anything to say, said it was no use saying anything.—The Chief Constable said the prisoner had been before the bench nine times. He would not work. He had respectable parents and a good home.—The magistrates committed him to prison for three months with hard labour on each charge. The prison•a• on leaving the box said "My aunt has done this."

PEDDLING WITHOUT LICHNCE.—John Willisms and George Kevil, last from Manchester, were ch aged with acting as pedl trs without licences. —The Chief Constable said he was under the impression that the prisoners should have beert charged with bein.; in Buttermarket-st . with felonious la- tent. He (the Chief Constable) was in the streA named on Saturday evening when he saw the twl defendants. e noticed that they were strangers and he watche them for some time. Ile saw them stopping pas engers off ring a few lac -s and pencils for sale Theyoffered them chiefly to peo- ple who came from a public-hous,l, and pushed their wares under the roses of the people tin y stopped. One person had a wat..th and chain, and one of the pris.mers engaged his at- tention by offering some letd pencils whilst the othe; pri- soner pushed against the ran on Ole other side. He (the Chief Constable) instructed P.O Leonard to tßlce the men into custody and to see whetlar-r they ha,l hawkers licences. It was found that they had none.— The magisteates imposed a fine of be. and costs or in default, seven days imprison- ment.

A CASE FOR INQUIRY—JuIia Ann Shields, of Fillings Court, who has appeared before the macistrates on many occasions, was ‘thar4ed with being drunk and disorderly in Fennel-st. on Saturday night the hief Constalle said imprisonment. seemed odo the woman very liti 'e good, and he was convinced th st she was not of sound mind. He would ask for a remand in ord• r that sue might be examined. It was a pity to send her nintinually to prison. She had been in a lunatic asylum, and h r conduct whilst in the cells was certainly not. that of a person compass mostis —The magistrates remanded the prisoner for a week in ordor that she might be merle-ally examined. DRUNK A•D DISORDERLY.—James Klmlin, 34 Dial-st., was charged with being drunk and d•sorderly in Dial et. on Sun- day morning—P.C. Cooper proved the charge.—lt was the prisoner's first offence and the magistiates discharged him. ' —Ellen Lawton was charged with a similar offence in W ttkin-st —Mr. Taylor, P.C.A., stated that the prisoner had sizned the pledge oa four r.ccasions but ha, relapsed into drunkenness again. She was a fustian cutter at one of Mr Prates shops, and was a good worker when she kept from drink,—he now promised the Mayor to sign the p edge and keep it, who thereut on said he would give her another chance and discharg d her. ASSAULT BY A. DRUNKEN MAN —William Tulle, 22, Wel- lington-street. a tanner. was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Hall-street at 11.20 on Saturday night and also with assaulting William Dunbobbin --P.O. Bell stated that he was in Bridge-street on Saturday night in company with P.C. Cooper, when he received information that there was a disturbance in Mersev-street. He went there and saw the defendant with three or four other young men, and he was told in the presence of the prisoner, who was drunk, that he wan i the instigator of the bother. Witness toid him jo go home, but he only went a few yards and stopped in Hall- street. waiting for a man n tined Dunbobbin to pass. Dun- bobbin afterwards w-nt up Mersev-s'reet, and was stopped by the prisoner who struck him ahoui the face and ribs Dun- bobbin told him that it was the third tine the prisoner had laid in wait for him —Willie -n Danbobbin spoke to being assaulted by the p,isoner at the ti stated. 'The previous Saturthy night, the prisoner wounded him on the head. tie never spoke to the prisoner.—The Mayor : Didn't you provoke him in any way? Witness: No, sir.— The Mayor : It is a most monstrous thng trat a man cannot go about the streets without nting assaulted.—P.C. Cooper corroborated P.C. Bell's statement. The defendent stated that Dunbob%in threat -fled to vaccinate " him and his family. He admitted that he struck the cotnplainant the previous Saturday, but ho was trying to ' make it up " with him when the bother commenced. Thomas Hawkins and John Hattori gave ev.diince on behalf of the prisoner.—The Mayor said the magistrates were determined tit put a Stop to this kind of thing. The prisoner would be committed to prison for one month with hard labour without the option of a fine. .

ANoTHER SHOP-DOOR THEFT.—Michael Henry,who refusei to give any particulars concerning hi mielf, was charged with stealing from the shop of Ann Jack,on, Winwick-st ,a man's vest, value 4s. 6d., her property. The Chief Constable stated that the vest was being displayed near the doorway of the shop on Saturday It was seen there at mid-day, and about half-an-hour afterwards it was missed. Information was at once given to the polio •, and from enquiries made it was found that the pri,oner offefed the vest for sale at the shop of J hn Gibbous, Mersey-st. He had it in hf s hand,and in answer to the enquiry of Mrs Gibbons as to wnether it was his property, he said it was. He asked 3s. for it, but he was given 2s.and another vest. Detective Foster found the vest at the shop,and it was handed over to him. The detective went to Market Gate, and the prisoner passed him. :-2eeing that he answered the description givim of the man who had sold the vest, he took him into custody. On being charged with the theft he said that a man had given it him to sell. He (the Chief Constable) beiivecl the prisoner had recently been discharged from th army, but he refused to tell them. It would (nein she loss of his pension.- James Byrne, assistant , to Ann Jackson, 6, VVinwick-st. ; Catherine Gibbon, Mersey- at., and Det. Foster gave evidence in corroboratiou of to Chief Constable's statement.—The prisoner was committed to prison for 14 day's hard labour.

div.head: ROYAL MARRIAGE,
div.p: THE ROYAL MARRIAGE,

The wedding of Princess Maud of Wales and Prince Charles of Denmark took place in the chapel at Buck- ingham Palace on Wednesday, in the presence of an assembly rarely equalled for brilliancy even in t. ourt circles, mcluding as it did the Queen, the Prince and Priecess of Wales (the bride's parents), the Duke of York, and most of the other members of the Royal Family,many representatives of European dynasties,and the leaders of the British aristocracy and political life. The marriage service was read by the Archbishop of Canterbury,who had with him within the altar rails the Bishops ot London and Winchester and several other clergymen,and who delivered a brief address at the con- clusion of the rite. The wedding ring was the one of Welsh gold which was recently presented to the bride- groom. At the elme of the ceremony the marriage re- gister was attested by the Queen,the Prince and Princess of Wales and others. The numerous processions between Marlborough House and York House prior to the mar- riage were witnessed by many thousands of persons,who were delighted at the sight ot the bride in her splendour and received her with tremendous cheering. The newly wedded couple left Marltorough House early in the evening for Norfolk,where they are to spend their honey moon.

div.head: Ettter to the ebitor.
div.p: Ettter to the ebitor.
CONSERVATIVE CANDIDATE FOR LATCHFORD
FOR NEXT NOVEMBER.

Sir,—The very slack att,mdance which Mr. Percy Davies nas mae e at his committees, has made his party very lukewarm about him, and in fact, they may be said to have dropped him, although he is said to be willing to stand again for Latchford upon certain condi- tions. But another manihas,it is rumoured,been selected in the person of Mr. W. B. Robarts, of Wilderspool Brewery. I don't knew how this will suit the other Mr. Roberts who represents tr)e Whitecrosa Ward—two Richmonds so opposite in opinions and in other ways, may cause some curious developments. What I want to ask is, why cannot the Latchford Conservatives find some other cacdidate than a person connected with the liquor trade. Are there not already nine or ten mem- bersnf " the Trade "in the Council ? If so, surely there are sufficient to represent the drink section of the Con- servative party. We are not all of this persuasion, and I hope it may not be too late to alter this blunder—for a blunder it is.—Yours truly, A LA.TCHFORD VOTER.

div.head: RUNCORN CYCLE PARADE.
div.p: RUNCORN CYCLE PARADE.

Sir,—Please permit us through the medium of your valuable paper to acknowledge the services of all who so ably took part in the parade on Wednesday last. The hearty response made to the appeal upon all sides proves to that our cause was a good and "popular " one, receiving the " popular " support asked for. This grand result, financially and otherwise, most certainly, could not have been brought about without the untiring, skil- ful and painstaking efforts during the p tst few weeks of every individual processionist and as it is, of course, impossible LA thank each one individually we here take the opportunity of publicly doing r, and are confident that every one—like ourselves 'will be fully repaid by the admirable success attending the whole undertaking. —Yours truly, W. H. MACK . W. E. DUDLEY f Joint Secs.

div.head: WA.RRING-ToNIANS IN AMERICA.
div.p: WA.RRING-ToNIANS IN AMERICA.
INTERWIEW WITH MR. JAMES ROBERTS.

A few days ago there arrived in Warrington,after an absence of fifteen years in America, Mr. James Roberts, second sqn of Mr. John Roberts of the firm of Messrs. A. Waring and Company, tanners, Winwick-road. With the object of providing the readers of the " Examiner " with a few particulars respecting matters American, our reporter intq- viewed Mr. Roberts at his father's house. Mr. James Roberts appeared in the best of health and soiritstand has evidently been thorough!y acclimat- ised in the new country. His speech has the Ameri- can accent and in some other respects he might easily be mistaken for a native born Yankee. His readiness to be interviewed and to give informa- tion respecting the great country on the other side of the Atlantic were conspicuous American traits. "I suppose you are paying a visit to this town after a prolonged absense ? " said the interviewer. "Yes, it is 15 years since I left the shores of the old country to seek my fortunes in the new. I served my apprenticeship in Warring- ton with Messrs. Newell and Barker at their iron works in Haydock-street,and as I afterwards found it very difficult to make any headway in my trade here, I decided to try America. I have been there ever since,and have succeeded beyond my anticipa- tions. This is my first visit home, and I can assure you it was a great meeting for my father at the Liverpool landing stage when I arrived by the Cephalonia, bringing with me a second generation of Roberts's. "In what part of America have you resided ? " "For the greater portion of the time in Boston, Mas- sachusets. I commenced working there in a very humble position making packing boxes and packing them, but I have worked my way up until now I °comas' the positi on of designer and inventor for the S. A. Woods Machine Company, of Boston, who are manu- facturers of wood-working machinery. It has meant a great deal of hard work on my part, and diligent study in my spare hours. I have now about fifteen patents in the various machines manufactured by the firm I have mentioned." " Well, and what is your opinion of the Americans? "I believe there is not a better class of people any- , where. Unfortunately,America is the dumping ground I of the world, and becomes the home of many undesir- able citizens who cause a great deal of trouble, and to some extent give a wrong impression of the American people. As a rule the best positions in the States are occupied by Americans and Englishmen. I am sorry to say that we have note in Americ a representative bedy of Englishmen that do credit to their country. When the Americans do meet with a good Englishman they appreciate him. " What do you think of their recent action towards England with reference to the Venezuelan difficulty ?" "President Cleveland's message was certainly a mis- take. That yacht dispute in which Lord Dunraven played such a part, and the Venezeelan qoestion,created quite a sensation in America, and made the Americans very bitter at the time. I had some experience of it, and feeling ran so high that several men had to ha dis- charged from our works. The Americans are a very impulsive class of people, and in matters of that kind they are soon desirous of showing a sort of patriotism. With regard to Lord Dunraven,l don't think he will ever be treated with the same respect in America as formerly. But these matters are now being healed up, and the visit of the Ancient and Honourable Artillery and the Non- conformist pilgrims to this country are evidences of it." "And who is going to be the next president ?" "Oh, McKinley. The Democratic candidate is prac- tically an unknown man' and I feel sure that the presi- dential election at the fall of the year will result in McKinley being at the top. The American people will shortly he in the throes of a number of elec- tions. Just before I came away I was appointed on one of the award and city committees, , which do work somewhat similar to your ward e,oramittees here. In addition to the Presidential elec- tion, there is also the election of g rvernor for each state, the election of senators, and members of the House of Representatives. The last mentiored deal with matters connected with their own State. The elected members on these public bodiee are paid for their services, but the English system is the best, and is free from that cor- ruption which is certainly to be seen in America." Rave you had much experience in election matters in Boston?" "Two years ago, I was a Republican candidate for the Boston City Council, and although I didn't succeed in gaining the honner, I ran my opponent closer than had ever been the case before. I have been since asked to stand as a candidate for the House of Representatives, but am undecided Omit doing so. lam going back in August in time for the forthcoming elections. "Rave you met any Warringtonians whilst in America ? " " Only two--L,Mr. Henry Wbitham, and Mr. Bibby, of Warrington, who was paying a visit there. I showed them round Boston." "Do you think the States are a desirable place to emigrate to ? - " Well not now. America has been overrun, and the chances for success now for an emigrant are not equal to what they used to be. The American people at pre- sent are much intereetel in Cuba, and if the Spaniards will clear out, I should thiek Cuba would be a great , place for artisans. The young men in England have been neglected in the pest,ancl sufficient facilities in the way of technical education have not been provided for them. There is every opportunity for providing the I best technical education in America. The reeult has teen that in many trades they are ahead of England in improved methods, and although the American take all the credit for this much of it is really due to English- men who have gone there. "Well, now, Piet as a parting qiiestion, what impression does the" good old town" make upon you after so long an absence ? " I was grieved to see the large number of children run- ning about the s reets carrying beer. I should think I have seen as much drunkenness since I came here as I have seen for many a month in Boston. There they don't supply children or womon,andthe drinkine saloons are closed on Sundays and holidays. I be ve been greatly interested in the Ship Canal. and there is undoubtedly some splendid work in connection with it. Although I came here Aolely for a holiday, I have already sold a patent of mine for filing and setting handsaws to a Warrington firm, and before I leave,' think I shall have sold more." Just before leaving. Mr. Roberts showed our reporter a splendid field glass which had been peesented to him on his departure be the South Boston Aid Association " as a mark of respect."

div.head: INQUESTS AT WARRINGTON-
div.p: INQUESTS AT WARRINGTON-
A CARTER CRUSHED TO DEATH.

Mr. Brighonse, county coroner, held an inquest at the Warrington Infirmary on Friday morning on the body of John McCormick, a carter in the employ of Mr. Joseph Houghton, Woolston, who died on Wednesday from in- juries he received the previous day by being crushed between two vehicles in Mersey-et.—The first witness called was Mrs. Orme, of Mill House, Woolston, who stated that the deceased lodged with her. She never knew his relatives in Ireland. None ever came to see him, and he never went to them while he lodged with I her. He was a carter for Mr. Joseph Houghton, farmer, Woolston. He would be about 41 years of age. She last saw him alive about two o'clock on Tuesday after- noon, when in company with another man he went to Warrington with two horses and a lurry.—Francis Trig- ger, a young man, stated that he was in company with the deceased on the day in question. They were return- ing with the lorry laden with manure when the acci- dent happened. Witness was leading the chain horse, 1 and when they turned down Mersey-at. at the Warring- ton Bridge end they saw two carts standind OppOgn Mr. Stanley Carter's warehouse, and a handcart on the opposite side. Witness got between them all right with the chain horse, but the deceased who was in charge of the horse in the shafts was unable to keep his horse far enough on the off-side with the result that he was crushed between the shafts and one of the carts which was standing still. He did not think there was any- one to blame. It was an error of judgment on the part of the deceased. He was sober at the time.— James Grimshaw stated that he saw the lorry coming , along Mersey-street. It was loaded with manure and , was going at a rapid rate. It was going down an in- cline and the drivers seemed to have lost control. Two ' carts were standing near Mr. Carter's warehouse and there was a handcart on the other side. In endeavour- ing to get between them the deceased was crushed be- tween the tail end of the cart and the shafts of the

lurry. He was going too quickly at the time to get safely between the casts on both sides of the street. The heavy load going down the incline pushed the shaft horse along, and it slipped a little on the setts. There was no brake in use.— Joseph Houghton, farmer, Woolston, stated that de- ceased had worked for him about four years. He was well acquainted with horses. There was a brake on the lurry worked by a lever. They did not generally put the brake on except on going down steen inclines. After examining the lurry when it came home he was of the opinion that the "turn-table" of the lurry had not been oiled sufficiently. He told the deceased to oil it before he went out. —Nurse Doesors said the deceased was ad- mitted to the Infirmary at 6.30 on Tuesday evening, suf- fering from broken ribs and injury to the lungs. He died at 4 a.m. the following mornina.—lnspector Cox stated that the police did not attach blame to anyone.— The Jury returned a verdict of" Accidental death."
SHOCKING ACCIDENT AT BEWSEY FORGE

At the Borough Court on Friday afternoon. Mr. Brig- house, coroner, held an inquiry with reference to the death of William Kenwrieht, of Bowes-st., Warrington, eche died at the Infirmary on Monday, from injuries re- ceived at f!eweoy Forge, the same day. Mr. Rogersone of Her Majesty's Inspectors of Factories, was present, and Mr. Ath.rton was present on behalf of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles. Peter Kenwright, 11, Cheater-st., Warrington, said d- ceased was his nephew, and lived at Bowes-at. Deceased was an engine driver at the Forge. Witness worked at the same place,but was not present at the time of the accident. He saw deceased at the Infirmary. Deceased wanted to speak to him, but witness forbade him. If a brit broke at the works the deceased should stop the en- gine and then mend the belt. No man should put the belt on :while it was going at full speed. Deceased had been driving engines for thirteen or fourteen years. In answer to a juryman, witness said it was not safe for a man to stand on a twelve-inch beam in order to put a 1 belton the wheels as deceased had done.—By Mr. Rogers : He had never put belts on himself. He hid seen them put on, but the engine had been slowed down. Nurse Dobson said deceased was admitted into the Infirmary shortly before seven o'clock on Monday morn- g. His left foot was already off. Amputation was resorted to, but the deceased died during the day. He did not make any statement to her. John Martin, furnaceman at the forge stated that he spoke to the deceased about five minutes before the acci- dent occurred. He heard the deceast d shout and on looking up witness saw the deceased being wound round the shaft. Witness shouted to someone to stop the engine which was done. He afterwards brought the foreman roller on the B=o. Thomas Llewellyn, engineer at the works, stated that about 6.20 on Monday morning he was told that the dngine-driver was fast in the pulleys. He went there and found two workmen trying to release the deceased. He had been twisted round the shaft a number of times land his clothing was wrapped round the shaft. He was released and taken on the ambulance to the Infirmary. Witness afterwards went to the shaft and unwrapped the deceased's clothing which was fast to it. From the way he found it he was led to believe that the deceased's shirt had caught in the "studs"of the pulleys and he had then been twisted round. The deceased hed endeav- oured to put the strap on the pulley with his right hand and had fallen in doing so. On witness trying to put the belt on the pulley after the accident he found that the diseased had laced the belt too short and it would not go on. The deceased should have got up by means of a ladder but witness was told that deceased got up by the crane. The Coroner : Was there a ladder at hand.—Witness : There was a ladder there when I got there.—But would there be one there at the time ?—There would be one about somewhere.—Has the engine to be slowed down or stopped when % strap has to be put on ?—The engine should have been slowed down.—What is the ordinary speed of running ?-4bout 45 revolevions a minute.—At what speed would it have been safe to put a belt on ? About a quarter that speed.—l 4 the man supposed to put the belt on with his hands ?—Yes.—Don't they put it on with a tork P—ln some places they do, but not that particular belt.—ls it not dangerous to put a belt on a pulley with the hands even if the engine is slowed P—Not with a certain amount of care.—Can you understand the deceased climbing up the crane if there is a ladder P—No, I can not understand that.—Why should he go against the instructions of his foreman ?—The deceased's mate has told him repeatedly to put no belt on without the engines are running slowly. —What benefit wee it to put the belt on at full speed ?—I could not say unless it was in the interests of the men working to keep thorn from stopping.—By Mr, Rogers: Could you put the belt on when standing on the ladder P—No, sire—You would have to stand on a twelve inch plank in order to put it on ?—Yes. Have you ever had these studs filed down and made level with the collar ?—No sir, but I think it would he better if that were done.—ln answer to questions by the jury- men, Mr. Atherton, the manager of the works, who pro- duced plans of the place where the accident occurred, said that he had given strict instructions to the men never to put a belt on whilst the engine was going at fell speed. The man would be protected against the intimidation of the workmen in the mill to keep it go- ing. Even if the metal was ready to be rolled the man could slow down the engines until he had got his belt on again. Mr. Rogers addressing the jury said in his opinion the accident was entirely due to the man putting the belt on when the engine was working at full speed. He had brought out one point with reference to the projecting studs hut still these studs were some distance away from the shaft and under ordinary circumstances it would have been safe to put the belt on. He had suggested to the firm that all the studs should be filed down. U rider the factory acts it was illegal to approach env unfenced dangerous machinery, but if the engine went slow it ceased to be dangerous. The Coroner pointed out that it was nota case of an nexperienced man being engaged. In this. particular instance the man knew the rules and regulations and he had disobeyed them. In the first place he climbed up a crane,he then laced the belt too tight, and endeavoured to put it en the pulley whilst the engine was running at full speed. The jury retired to consider their verdict and on re- turning the foreman said the jury returned a verdict of Accidental death," and recommended that there should be some protection of the projecting studs, and also that there should be some provision for getting at ho pulleys easier.

A MAN KILLED BY A FALL OF EARTH. At noon on Friday, Mr. Brighouse held an inquest with reference to the death of Robert Roscoe, 34 years of age, of Woolston, who died at Rixton on Tues- day, from injuries received a short tima before :by the falling of rubbish upon him while as- sisting in the widening of the Glazebeook-lane, Glaze- brook.--Mr. A. E. White (clerk to the Warrington High- way Board), Mr. Thompson (surveyor), and Captain Withington were present on behalf of the Warrington District Highway Board. Ann Roscoe, wife of the deceased, stated that he had worked for the Highway Board about two years. She identified the body. John Thompson, surveyor, said the Board was taking down a bank in Glazebrook-lane about seven feet high and it was being brought down. in " benches " of from fifteen to eighteen inches high. The ground was sandy and gravel with clay at. the top. The work was unaer the supervision of William Bate. Witness had seen the place before, the accident. Bate was an experienced man in such work.

He had been employed by the Board for twenty years. He never expected anything of the kini to happen. There were about 48 yards of the hank removed, and there had been some difficulty in cutting it through.

William Bate, foreman Of the men", said he was in charge of the work of zutting through the bank, which was a little over six feet high. The deceased was about six feet in height. Between 9 and 930 o'clock on Tues- , day morning the deceased,Peter Roberts and Henry Ash- ton were engaged to cut under the bank While the three men were working witness saw the bank suddenly crack and shouted "Look sir." Roberts and Ashton got clear, , but deceased was forced on the edge of the bank and knocked down and covered with earth. He was speedily got out and complained of pains in the middle part of the body. Mrs. Bridge who was passing in a trap took the - deceased with her with the intention of driving him to the Warrington Infirmary, but he died on the way. Witness never expected the bank to go down as it did. John Platt, another workman, said he was fifty yards away when the bank fell. Ho assisted to get the de- ceased out.

Peter Roberts gave similar evidence. The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death," 'and txpressed sympathy with the relatives of the de- ceased. Mr. White said he wished also to convey the sympathy of the Board with the relatives. They re- gretted the occurrence, and it was the first which had happened since the Board came into existence thirty years ago.

BAILIFFS AND RIGHT OF ENTRY. ALLEGED B UTING AN ASSISTANT. CURIOUS CASE. On Friday at the Warrington Berough Court, before Alderman Harrison, Alderman Wright, Couneillers Pierpoint and Roberts, and Mr. S. Wright, Benjamin and Mrs. Hampson, 255 Knutsferd-road were charged with assaulting William Burrows, 15, Upper Bank-street, on the 26th June. Mr. H. J.Longton prosecuted and Mr. A. Browne defended. Mr. Longton said, that on Friday the 26`h June, Bur- rows, the complainant, in company with Mr. Frain, and an assistant, Newall went to defendant's house in Hants- ford-road, Latchford, to levy a distress warrant for rent. They went to the front door and that was fast and they could not get in. They then went to the bards darer which was open and told the defendant they had a warrant for execution for distress for rent and he said" You are too late " and got hold of Burrows by the neck to throw him out. Burrows coat was torn in the struggle. Mrs. Hamp- son was in the back of the premises and she hissed a dog on to bite Burrows. The dog flew at Burrows and seized him by the leg, and bit him in two places and tore his trousers. Frain said " Now its no use," and called Newall, who said" Shall I hit the dog "and Frain paid " Certainly." Newell then hit it and the dog loosed his hold. Frain remonstrated with Hampson who said to his wife " call the dog off." He submitted that bailiffs should be protected in the execution of their duty. William Burrows corroborated the statement that Mrs. Hampson set the dog at him. His leg bled and he had to go to the doctor. Cross-examined by Mr. Browne: He was not a certi- ficated bailiff. Mr. Roberts: Has he any right, not being a certific- ated bailiff, to enter the house. Mr. Browne : Not the slightest. That is my point. We also allege that Burrows was drunk. Burrows : I was not. Mr. Browne : We say Burrows was trespassing in the house. Persons not duly certificated have no right to go and distrain. Burrows said he had the warrant himself when he went in. Mr. Browne: Then you had no right. Mr. Longtnn : He was there with Frain. Mr. Roberts: Your own evidence shows that this was the man who made the entrance with the warrant. Mr. Longton : A person has a right to employ assist- ants. Mr. Roberts: The law says these warrants must be executed by a duly certificated man. Mr. Langton : I submit he was with Frain and Frain has a right to have assistance. Mr. Roberts : There is a proper and an improper way and this is the improper way. So far as this case is concerned I think it is at an end. I think your own evidence proves that Burrows was a trespasser and that therefore any man was right in chucking him out. Thoma s Frain, 28, Bsevsey-read, Warrington, certifi- cated bailiff.said they walked in at the back door which was open. Burrows was a few yards in front, and Hampson said "You are too late," being under the impression that they could not enter after 6 o'clock. Mrs. Hampson hissed the dog at Burrows. Hampson subsequently became very reasonable. Cross-examined: Barrows had the warrant but they were both in at the same time. He did not tell Sergeant Smith he was in another house when Burrows came to execute the warrant. Hampson was trying to turn Burrows out. Burrows did not go into the front room and rummage in the drawees. Witness gave the war- rant to Burrows to get in first if he could. Mr. Pierpeint : Was not there a difference between the amount on the rent book and that on the warrant. Mr. Frain : There was, but that often occurs. Mr. Pierpoint : Was it in favour of the tenant. Mr. Frain : I believe it was. I think there was more on the warrant than on the rent book but it was not Our error. George Newell, 51 Nicholson-street, assistant bailiff, said that on the thy ,n question he went in company with Frain and Burrows to Latchford. The front door of defendant's house was locked and witness and Mr. Frain went together to the back where Hampson had Burrows by the threat trying to push him out. He hoard Mrs. Hampson say "At him Jack," to the dog. He hit the dog by Frain's permission and went with Burrows to Dr. Smith. Cross-examined : 111 r. Frain was going down the en- try when he was. When they got to the back Hampson was trying to push Burrows through the door. Mr. Browne : I submit that the last witness has en- tirely put the case out of court. Alderman Harrison : We are trying a case of assault. Mr. Browne : Yes,but Hampson was perfectly justified in putting him out. Mr. Lony,ton : I think Mr. Frain ought to be called on that point before any allegations are made. Mr. Frain, in answer to the Bench : He was perfectly sober. I think mole s ,ber than ever I knew him. (Laughter.) Mr. Browne (to the Chairman) : How many titres has veur worship sacked Burrows for drunkenness? Mr. Fain : I cannot say, sir. Mr. Brewne said Burrows rushed into defesdant's house *and went to the parlour door. Ha,mpsion pushed him back and Burrows got hold of the towel and rail and snatched it down. Defendant was just putting him out when Frain came up. Frain had sent Burrows round to the back while he tried the front. This —a, a common trick. Ngwall had stated that when 'hey g)t to the back Hampson had Burrows by the no, k T cleat ly showed that Burrows was in front. He he i no right to have the warrant. Another matter was that the dog's name was not Jack. Burrows rummaged in the drawer and put his fist in Mrs. Hampson's face. The magistrates decided that Burrows had no right to distrain. Alderman Harrison, addressing Mr. LonF,,ton, said the majnrity of the magistrates were entirely against him. He himself was dead against their opinion. Burrows was technically wrong in being first, but Frain was there. The gentlemen on both sides of him disagreed with him, and he had no alternative but to dismiss the case.

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, JULY 25, 1996.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, JULY 25, 1996.
WARRINGTON.
WARRINGTON HORSE AND CATTLE FAIR.

The usual half-yearly fair was held on Friday and Saturday last week. There was a poor attend- ance of buyers, and there was little business done. Prices of cows, milkers, .El 6 to .E2O; barrens, £8 to £l2; springers, £l2 to £l5. Horses, heavy, £4O to £5O; harness, £2O to .E3O; ponies, £lO to £l6. ALLEGED THEFT FROM A WARRINGTON TAN. William Rigby, of Platt Bridge, who was stated to have served five years' penal servitude for rob- bery with violence, was charged at Wigan, on Saturday, with stealing an overcoat from the Wigan market-square, the property of John Ainsworth, a fowl dealer, of Warrington. Prosecutor had a stall in the market, and left his overcoat behind a crate. During the day prisoner met a constable, and Oe officer noticing that the man had an overcoat in his possession, and that he ran away immediately on seeing him, chased him and eventually captured him. When asked where he had got the coat from prisoner said he did not know, but subsequently admitted that he had stolen it. Prisoner was com- mitted for trial at the Liverpool ASFiZeS.

SCHOOL TREAT AT DARESBURY. The scholars attending the Daresbury Board Schools were on Friday given their annual tea party provided from the proceeds of a concert held in the school during the winter months. About 230 arrived at the school at three o'clock, and at once' com- menced amusing themselves with cricket, swings, &c.,in a field placed at their disposal by Mr. Billing- ton, of the Village Farm. Here, the weather being most favourable, the children partook of an excel- lent tea, after which sports, consisting of egg and spoon races, obstacle and flit races, &c.,, for which money prizes were given, were eagerly contested. At seven o'clock the Preston Brook Brass Band ar- rived on the scene, and did themselves great credit with the music discoursed, to which dancing by the parents and relatives of the scholars took place un- til dusk, whdn after nuts, s seete, and a bun had been distributed to each child ell dispersed.

div.head: ADJOURNED INQUEST ON A NEWTON BOY.
div.p: THE ADJOURNED INQUEST ON A NEWTON BOY.

SWALLOWING A PIECE OF WIRE. On Friday afternoon Mr. S.Brighouse,County Coroner, conducted the adjourned enquiry into the circumstances of the death of James Barran, aged 9, son of James Barran, Newton-le-Willows, who died on the 28th June, from the effects of swallowing a small piece of wire,sup- posed to have been concealed in bread the child had
aten. Mr. Longton again appeared for the baker of the bread and Mr. J. P. Mearns, St.. Helens appeared for
the relatives of the deceased boy
The -thief Con-
stable and Inspector Spinks were also present. Dr. Elarold Watkins now appeared and gave evidence
Mr. Brighouse read over the evidence given by bite witnesses at the previous hearing. James Barran, senior, examined by Mr. Mearns. said

they gave the boy a pill every four hours and he com- plained that he could not take thetn. Dr. Watkins said if he had to operate on the by he would have to remain with him and that ho_ could not. This was on Sunday
night, a week after the boy swallowed the pin. 'fhey had confidence in the doctor, and he recommended that the boy be taken to the Infirmary. Mrs. Elarran, ex mined by the coroner. sairi the boy

lived nine days after the swallowing of the wire. She took the boy to Dr. Watkins on the Saturday morning and he was examined but the doctor could find nothing. He gave them some medicine to " gargle " his throat. She took him again on Sunday but the doctor said he could see nothing but a scratch. Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday passed and the deceased was quiet. Dr. Watkins saw him again on Thursday and changed the medicine. Witness took deceased again on Saturday night and he gave witness mare medicine and some Pniment to bring out the abscess. She got a box of 12 pills on Saturday night. The first pill was given on Saturday night and others every foal. hours. The boy cried every time she had to give the pills to him. Ott Sunddy, Dr. Watkins saw the boy twice. The first time on Sunday he advised them to take the boy to Warring- ton Infirmary. He suggested nothing of that kind previously. By Mr. Mearnes : The doctor's house was near wit- , ness's. There were two practising doctors in Newton. Dr. Watkins said he could do the operation himself but he was single-handed and might be called out any minute. In the nine days Dr. Watkins examined the boy twice. He could find nothing but a scratch- and some little ulceration. She thought the boy unfit to be taken to Warrington and he cried for the cab-windows to be opened on the way. The boy died as he was being carried into the Infirmary. Mr. W. Roberts (a juryman) : I should like to know distinctly what the doctor said on Sunday night. Witness at first could not remember but on being re- minded by the Coroner said he told her there would be no need for her to see him again until the medicine was done. Dr. Langdale, examined by Mr. Mearns said if he thought it was desirable he would have administered the pills. If he was told a patient's throat was made up he could not say whether he would have given pills. Some doctor's used pills much more than others. If the de- ceased bad said the pill stuck in his throat he thought his mother might hesitate about giving the next. de was unable to say whether Dr. Watkins could have learned the state of the throat, as discovered after death. The Coroner : The real point is whether the doctor could have found that it was wrong to administer the pills to the child. Do you think there was such evi- dence as would justify any man in not giving pills,as be- ing dangerous to its life? Dr. Langdale said the evidence all seemed to show that the child's difficulty in breathing was of rapid develop- ment. He gathered that the child's general symptoms were not generally alarming when the pills were ordered. The Coroner said Dr. Harold Watkins had voluntarily written a statement upon the circumstances of the deceased's illness and death. The statement, which the Coroner read aloud, was to the effect that the patient was first brought to the doctor between 10 and on the 20th June, 1896, with the state- ment that while eating he had swallewed a pin. On examination he could see nothing nor could he find anything by using his finger or the gullet probes. He informed the child's mother of the fact and that it was 'possible that symptoms complained of were caused by I some hard substance being swallowed and instructed her to bring the boy the blowing day if he complained. She brought him again at 8 o'clock on the fist and wit- ness made another examination of the throat hut could not detect anything beyond a small and probably old ulcer. He nave medicine to be taken every four hours land to last 32 hours. Dr. Watkins here added in Court I that it was Tuesday or Wednesday before he saw the child again and the medicine should have been finished at Monday midnight. He told deceased's mother to come svlien it was done. He afterwards learned that the mother thought the boy was to have a teaspoonful, whereas the bottle was marked 1-Bth every 4 hours. Mrs. Ilarran next brought the boy to him on Thursday and the neck was then swollen, but not the throat. He gave medicine to last 48 hours and deceased was again brought on Saturday, and the swelling was about the same. The inside of the left of the throat was a bit swollen and there was paralysis of the left side of the larynx. He gave instructions that the pills which he gave were to be placed in honey or crushed if there was any difficulty about swallowing them. They were to reduce the swelling on the neck. Witness next saw the deceased about 10 30 a.m. on Sunday the 27th May and told Mrs. Flarran to discontinue the pills if they heft the lad. The difficulty in breathing then was due to the peralysis.Deceased had then taken four pills but it was impos ible for- him (-he doctor) to have told that they had not passed through the throat. He advised that the boy be sent to Warrington Infirmary for an operation of tracheotomy and at 1.25 he saw the boy aeain,and again advised his going to Warrington and he was siitiequently taken and arrived at 3inog'cwloacs affected.k . He could not do it then as he might have been called any minute to another very serious case. The boy was quite fit to be taken on Sunday to War- rington. Witness had during the time he had been at Newton removed half-a dozen pins from the throats of people. As to the advisability of giving pills, the same drug could have been taken in three ways. He decided that the pills were the easiest form in an inflamma- tory case. Mr. Bewcock (a jeryman) : Why did you not send for medical men from Ear estown to do the operation. Dr. Watkins said they were generally absent on busi- ness on Sunday moreings. Ho sent the boy to Warrington as the best place for ensuring immediate treatment. Joseph Sharp (foreman to Mr. Melyneux), the baker who supplied the Ha ren's with bread, said no machin- ery was used in its manufacture. He thought if the pin or wire had been in it it would have been discovered by the men. Great precautions were taken. div.head: TRIAL OF DR. JAMESON.
div.p: THE TRIAL OF DR. JAMESON.

The trial of Dr. Jameson and the other leaders in the raid on the Transvaal was begun at the Royal Courts of Justice on Monday. It is a trial "at bar," and the judges are the Lord Chief Justice,Mr. Baron Pollock,and Mr. Justice Hawkins. Before the special jury em- panelled was sworn Sir Edward Clarke, the leading counsel for the defence, moved that the indictment be ' quashed. He argued that there was a fatal uncertainty in the allegation r specting the operation of the Foreign Enlistment Act, which did not come into force outside the United Kingdom unless it had been made the subject of a proclamation. Their Lordships reserved their de- cision on the point till next morning, and the court ad- journed. When the Court reassembled on Tuesday morning the Lord Chief Justice said that he and his brother judges had considered the objections to the indictment taken by Sir Edward Clarke, and had come to the conclusion that none of them ought to prevail. A jury was then empanelled,and the case was proceeded with. The At- torney General went into detail as to the status of the South African Republic and the relation in which it stood to the British Government, and said it seas the duty of every person concerned with governing powers in South African territory to respect such status and re- lation. The trial of Dr. Jameson and his principal comrades was continued on Wednesday, the evidence, as given before the magistrate, of several persons who took part in the expedition being now repeated.
