div.head: NOTES AND NEWS.
div.p: NOTES AND NEWS.

We are told that a special feature in thisyear's German manceuvres will be supplied by war dogs which have been most admirably trained for seeking the wounded and carrying despatches. At the command " seek," accompanied by a gesture indicating the direction in which the dogs are to search, they will start off; they will find the men who figure as wounded with unfailing certainty, take a piece of their clothing—cap, helmet, or piece of cloth torn off, and bring this back to the ambul- ance men, whom they then conduct to the spot.

In the" Figaro " M. Guibert relates an interview he had in Paris with Li Hung Chang. "1 know," Li said (according to the" Daily News" report)," that public Opinion in a force in the West, and that papers direct Opinion." Li is not for liberty of the press in China.and looks with no favourable eye on pavers published in Chinese at Hong Kong or Shanghai. " What most struck you about France 2" "Her wealth. It is tremendous. Your provinces seem more sparsely plpu- lated than China, but content and well-being seem to prevail everywhere. And then France is a country of

_ literary and scientific .1-i.en." -Li desires to appoint a European doctor for the Imperial family, but has been unable to overcome Court prejudice. Ten years ago he was cured of incipient paralysis 01 the brain by Mr. Irving,an Englishman,Chinese science having been of no avail. "What do you think of the English ? " I ap- preciate the English, I like (or love) the French." On hts visit to German factories Li was very reticent, and when his visitors attempted to draw from him a state- ment on general policy for the regeneration of China,Li cut short the interview. He rose, shook hands, and said " I love the French. I have come to their country to show it, say it, and also prove it." To another visi- tor Li said China would welcome foreign capital and knowledge, but would not favour either England or France at the expeiase of the others. As for purchases in Europe or America, China waaild buy in the cheapest market.

One of the strongest men of the 25,000 Norwegian fishermen that assembled off Loff.iden this summer was a Norwegian fisherman, who is reported to be eighty-six Norwegian inches in height, ani of unusually strong build. In a race recently rowed against a boat crow containing five rowers, this worthy descendant of the old Norsemen came in first. The Norwegian is going to be dressed up as an ancient Viking and exhibited by his admiring countrymen. The preceeds of this novel ex- hibition are to go towards the maintenance of the life- boat stations along the coast of Norway.

The Pope has recently been presented with an interesting gift, a typewriter. It is a very elaborate and magnificent specimen, being inlaid with ivory and silver. The Papal arms have also been introduzed in irs decorations with excellent effect. His Holiness, on re- ceiving it, examined it with interest, but remarked with a sly smile that although he would have it used by some- body who understood its mechanism, he thought he was himself too old to learn. Among the Pope's scientific toys none amuses him, it seems, more than his phono- graph, which contains a rare collection of voice-plates, including several of those of his deceased friends. By means of this elaborate phonograph, the Pope has heard Madame Patti sing " Home Sweet Home," and likewise the voices of Mr. Gladstone and of the two Presidentsiof the United States.

A grateful country spent enormous sums of money in providing for the first Duke of Marlborough and his descendants. 'the "St. James's Gazette," speaking of a recent visit of the Duke of Marlborough to Windsor, says it was partly of a lonsiness character. In accord- ance with the grant in Petit Serjeanty by which he holds his palace aud lands of Blenhaim, he is bound to present to the Sover,ign on Angus 13, the anniversary of the battle of Blenheim, a small French standard—that is, a replica of the Bourbon flag of the lilies. As it happens. however, the Queen is never at Windsor in August, and she does not care for visits from subjects at Osborne. She therefore sends a command to the Duke to. visit Windsor at a convenient period like the present, and the business of offering the standard, is formally accom- plished at a suitable interval. The standard is hung in the Guardroom over the portrait of John Churchill, first j Duke of Marlborough.

In a letter:written at Bulawayo in June an Englishman who has made some investments in Matabeleland, and who appears to think, like a certAin American judge in the days of slavery, that a black man has no rights which a white man is bound to respect, says :—" I fear this country will be no good for the next two years. The war drags on slowly, and now again there is a scarcity of meat in camp, and wheat there is 29. to 29. 6t per pound. I own a lot of good ground, but heaven alone knows when it will he ioated, if ever. To-day the news . of the Makalakas rising Mashonaland is confirmed, and wild reports are current that the Gazaland tribes and the Barotses are. moving to help them. That the latter tribe are MOVIEtg Is most unlikely, for they and the Matabele are hereditary enemies. Some men blame the Company for the business in the Transvaal, but most men, I think, know the Boer and the Hollander,and hate them as they hate a Matabc le rebel. More one can- not say. What will be the outcome of the whole business no one knows. If there is not now a row with the Trans- vaal, sooner or later there will be, and probably sooner rather than later. With regard to the Matabele, they talk here now of holding them back by chains of forts. Abs.lute rubbish. The country will never be safe for the white prospector and miner till the Matabele get such a terrible lesson that they will never again dare speak too loudly in the presence of a white man."

Of all the intrepid spirits who have of late conspired to beleaguer the North Pole, Mr. Andrea at. present I commands the chief share of the world's attention. His attempt to reach the Pole in a balloon makes a strong appeal to the imagination, and so far—but,of course, he is as yet only in the initial stages—fortune has favoured him. It is true that he has concili Ited fortune to some tune. His plans have been well laid, even to the warn- ing of the natives over whose territory he proposes to pAss,through the agency of the Hudson's Bay Company, that they must not be scared by a vision in the sky. Mr. Andiel reached Iseford, SpitZbergen, on the 20th June. rwo days later he ostablishad himself at Pike's House,in the northern half of West Spitzbergen,oppoSite Dane's Island, and was able then to report that he had already disembarked most of his stores. In the letter, written from Pike's House, which has just been received by a friend in Stockholm, Mr. Andree says that he ex- pects tc start for the Pole in three or four weeks. Not for thirty years has the ice been in such favourable con- dition. " All on board," he says, "are in the best of spirits. To ohne of us the idea occurs that we may meet serious difficulties." The scheme is bold enough to suc- ceed, and if Mr. Andr6 were to accomplish something really great we should not have to confess to great sur- prise.

A remarkable character in the person of Josephine, widow of M. Rostkowsky, believed to be the oldest cen- tenarian in France, has died at Aniche, near Douai, at the ago of 112 years and 4 months. Her husband was a captain in the 6th Polisn Regiment of the Line, and she herself took part in numerous engagements as aasistant surgeon. It is added that at the age of seventy-one she took part in the Crimean War in the rank, of the French Army.

DRUNKENNESS.
At the Earlestown police station on Monday morning before Mr. J. W. Emmett, Michael Melvin, of B,ubins Row, was charged with being drunk on the Saturday night, and was fined 2s. 6d. and Costs.

div.head: ACCIDENT TO A BOY.
div.p: ACCIDENT TO A BOY.

On Saturday a boy named William Slinn, 7 years of age, son of Mr. G. Shun, Haydock-street, Earles- town, fell out of a van belonging to Mr. P Thomp- son, grocer. Bridge-street, and sustained a fractured arm. Dr. Valentine set the injured limb.

div.head: IS lIWTON RACES.
div.p: IS lIWTON RACES.

The races this year at Newton will be held on Friday and Saturday. All the works in the neigh- bourhood, including the collieries at Haydock will leave work on Thureday night until Monday morn- ing. Many of the employes at the Viaduct works, taking advantage of the holiday, will avail them- selves of the privilege of the quarter fare ticket, and journey to various popular places.

div.head: SOCIAL .EVENINO.
div.p: SOCIAL .EVENINO.

The teaelers of St. John's Church Sunday school and several friends, numbering altogether about 30, had a swial evening in the Mission Hall, Earles- town, on Tuesday evening. An enloyabieP tea was provided, Aiss Clayton and others being responsible, and the remainder of the evening was spent in singing &c.

NEWTON RACE SUNDAY. Sunday last was what at one time was popularly known as Race Sunday. In years gone LI, the vicinity of Newton Common was fairly well crowded with various kinds of amusements, which were well patronised, Large numbers of people drove over from the outlying districts, and the day was practically given over to boisterous amuse- ments. All tons has now been abolished, and a visitor to the Common would not observe anything out of the ordinary, except for thte preparations being made for the races. ACCIDENT TO A PROVISION VAN.

On Saturday morning when the EArlestown Co-operative Society's van and horse were being driven down Wargrave-road, on the usual round, the britchen chain broke when the van was passing under the railway bridge. The horse stu bled,and the shafts fell to the ground, causingsa young lad who was in the van to be thrown out, and sustain an injury to his shoulder. The provisions with which the van was loaded were scattered about the road, and a quantity damaged.

div.head: ST. JOHN'S CHURCH, EARLESTOWN.
div.p: ST. JOHN'S CHURCH, EARLESTOWN.

On Sunday; a Flower Service took place in the above church, in aid ot the annual Sunday school treat. The service in the morning was conducted by the Rev. T. R. Matthews, and in the evening by the Rev. E. W. W. Kaye, who also addressed the children in an appropriate manner, on flowers. A large number ot children handed in offerings of flowers, &e., and they were received by the clergy at the communion rails. An anthem was sung by the choir, Miss Conway taking the solo. The flowers were subsequently sent to the Haydock Cottage Hospital, and Warrington Infirmary. The collec- tions amounted to £5 6s. 60.

div.head: WAGONETTE ACCIDENT AT BARLESTOWN.
div.p: WAGONETTE ACCIDENT AT BARLESTOWN.

On Friday nigt:t a wagonette belonging to Mr. Haskins, Earlestown, was conveying a number o people from 13.aydock to Earlestown, for marketing purposes, and when turning into Vista-road, it, from some cause or other overturned. All the passengers were thrown out but fortunately none of them Were injured beyond a few scratches. It is sup- posed that the driver turned too suddenly, or the wheels came in contact with the curbstone, and the fact of none of the people being injured is ac- counted for by the wagonette turning over grad- ually.
VIADUCT INSTITUTE BOWLING CLUB
In connection with - the above club a handicap

took place on the Institute bowling green, &tries- town, on ,Saturday afternoon. There was a large number of entries, the first prize being a copper kettle given by Mr. Astley King. After a very ex- citing struggle with Mr. T. Compton, the firit prize was secured by Mr. McAteer. The second prize a set of carvers, was taken by Mr. Compton, third prize,half a dozen desert knives,Mr. J. Finch. The prizes were distributed by the Secretary, and a hearty vote of thanks was accorded Mr. King for providing the members with a pleasant afternoon's sport.

div.head: ACCIDENT TO A NEWTON FARMER.
div.p: ACCIDENT TO A NEWTON FARMER.

On Saturday afternoon Mr. Thomas Williams, of New Hay Fartn,Newton-le-Willows, met with a pe- culiar accident,by which he sustained a fracture of two ribs. Mr. Williams,who is over 70 years oi age, was attending to a cow in the shippon when it somehow knocked him down, and he fell against the feet of a cow in an adjoining stall. This latter cow being startled became restive, and strained at its head chain, causing it to fall, and unfortunately it fell upon Mr. Williams. Some minutes elapsed before he was found, when he was picked up and catried into the house. Dr. Valentine was sent for, and he found that Mr. Williams had two ribs broken as stated. Pie was medically attended to, and is now progressing favourably.

GOOD TEMPLARY. The "'weekly session of the Hope of Elrlestown Lodge of Good Templars was held in the Co-onera- tive Hall on Monday evening. Bro. G. Clarke, c.T., presided, and there was a good attendance of mm- hers and visitors from Ashton Excelsior Lodge. fwo• candidates were initiated. It was resolved to give a sacred entertainment at Ashton Excelsior Lodge on Sunday,August 9th. Arrangements for holding the quarterly session of the District Lodge in Earles- town on August 22nd were made. The programme of tne evening was "a night of harmony, Sistars S. ' Caldwell (A Secretary), M. Jackson (R), and Bro. A. Howarth (pianist), being responsible. The follow- ing programme was submitted ;—Ode, "Always cheerful;" song,"Robin Adair,"Brother W.Crowther; song, " Owd Pinder," Bro. John Warburton; duet, "Home, beautiful home," Sisters Jackson and Cald- well ; recitation," A tragic story," Sister A. Jack- son; song," Daddy," Sister C. Smith ; duet, "The pilot brave," Bros. W. H. Crowther and G. Clarke. Thanks to the committee for their efforts termin- ated the meeting.

WEDDING AT EARLESTOWN. A.t the Wesleyan Chapel, Earlestown, on Tuesday afternoon, Miss Isabella Houston Blair, third daughter of Mr. Walter Blair, a foreman at the Viaduct Works, Earlestown, residing in Market- St., was marriedi to Mr. Ernest Downs, grocery and provision dealer, Earlestown. The bride was attired in a cream alpaca dress, trimmed with pearls, with bat to match, and carried a large bouquet of choice flowers, her ornaments being a gold bangle, the gift of the bridegroom. The bridesmaids were Miss Lizzie Blair (sister of the bride), and Miss Johnstone (cousin), the former ' wearing a pale blue cashmere dress, and the latter a pale green cashmere dress, both wore white hats, and a gold brooch, the gift of the bridegroom and they carried bouquets of flowers. The best man was Mr. Walter Downs, cousin of the groom. The ceremony was performed by the R9V. J. Bartley, the bride being given away by her father, and the service was choral,Mr. T. Gilmour presiding at the organ. After the ceremony the happy couple left for Scotland where the honeymoon will be Spent. The presents were numerous and co-01y, numbering over sixty, among them being a China tea service and Wedgewood tea-pot, the gift oi the teachers at the Wesleyan school, where the bride was a teacher for about 10 years.

IMPEIIIAL PARLIAMENT. MONDAY. The House of Commons on Monday considered the Lords' amendments to the Manchester Ship Canal Bill, and agreed to them. Several questions were addressed to Mr. Curtzms in re- ference to the recent events in Crete and Armenia, but little information beyond what was already known was elicited. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN answered a series of questions in reference to the Chartered Company and its territory. To Mr.Arnnld-Foster he said he did not think it a favour- able time when a rebellion was in progress to consider • alterations in the machinery of administration. TUESDAY. Mr. MACLEAN asked On Cuesday in the HOREB Of Com- mons whether the Government would consider the ex- pediency of opening negotiations with a view to the con- struction of a line through Candahar and Herat, to be connected with the Russian railway system. Mr. CURZON replied that it was premature at present to go into the matter. In answer to Mr. Luttrell and Mr. Scstt, the Colonial Secretary said he had had no official confirmation of the report from Bulawayo that Native Commissioner Thomas had destroyed about 1,000 bags of grain belonging to the natives, that famine was impending, and that even if the natives surrendered there was net food enough in Bulawayo to feed them for a single day. Mr. CHAMBER- LAIN added that if the people submitted he bad no doubt every effort would be made to save them from starva- tion. Replying to Mr. Mac Neill, Mr. CHAMBERLAIN said there must have been some error of transmission in the message which stated that the Select Committee of the Cape House of Assembly had found as a fact that the Char- tered Campauy supplied the funds for the Jameson raid. Sir W. HARCOURT intimated that the Opposition de- sired to have debates on the questions of South Africa and Venezuela,and Mr. Balfour undertook to try to come to some arrangement with then. The House went into Committee on the Irish Land Bill, taking up clause 7, to which Mr. G. Balfour had moved an amendment. Part lof the Bill was disposed of and Part 2, relating to the Land Commission, was entered upon. WEDNESDAY. The House of Commons on Wednesday resumed the Committee stage of the Irish Land Bill, and at a very early stage the Government suffered defeat. Clause 24 provides that advances to purchaw rs under the Bill shall be in cash, instead of, as hitherto, in guaranteed land stock, which now stands in the market at £llO per £lOO. Sir T. Esmond° moved as an amendment that advances should continue to be made in stock. This was supported by all sections of the Nationalist party, and also by the representatives if the landlords. Mr. G. Balfour contended that the effect would be to place a burden on the guarantee fund, and ultimately on the ratepayers of Ireland. Mr. A. J. Balfour objected to bonuses being given to facilitate land purchase, and asked all lovers of sound finance to support the Govern- ment. On a divisien there were 99 for the amendment and 88 against. the Government being thus defeated by 13 votes. Mr. Balfour then asked that the clause should be negatived for the present,and this was done.
